text: 1.1. Next it would be in place to take up — since the Scripture called the Greeks thieves of the barbarian philosophy — how this is to be shown in brief. For we shall set forth that they not only record, by imitating, the marvellous things of those things recorded among us, but that they fabricate and falsify the most authoritative of the doctrines, our Scriptures being older, as we have demonstrated; and we shall convict them in the matters concerning faith, and concerning wisdom and knowledge and science and hope and faith, and concerning repentance and self-control, and indeed the fear of God (a very swarm of the virtues of truth, of which as many as the present treatment of the subject requires will be taken in); and that especially the hidden part of the barbarian philosophy, this symbolic and enigmatic kind, was emulated by those who in earnest philosophized the things of the ancients, as a thing most useful, or rather most necessary, to the knowledge of the truth.

1.2. Upon this it is fitting, I think, to make a defence concerning the things for which the Greeks run us down, using a few Scriptures — if perhaps the Jew too, listening quietly, may be able to turn from the things in which he believed to him in whom he did not believe. And there will fittingly follow, for the noble of the philosophers, a refutation made in love, both of their life and of the discovery of their new doctrines — we not requiting our accusers (far from it, who have learned to bless those who curse, even if they vainly bring blasphemous words against us), but for the turning of those very men, if perhaps the all-wise might be ashamed, brought to soberness by a barbarian refutation, so as to be able, late at least, to discern what those studies are, on account of which they undertake their journeys overseas. For of what they are thieves — and indeed these things too must be demonstrated, once their self-love is taken away — and of what they, having searched, boast that they themselves found out — the refutation of these. And, as a consequence, we must run over also the so-called cyclic education, in how far it is useful, and over astrology and mathematics and magic and sorcery. For the all-Greeks pride themselves on these too as the greatest sciences. But he who reproves with frankness makes peace.

1.3. We have said already many times that we have neither studied nor practise speaking elegant Greek; for this is enough to lead the many away from the truth. But the true philosophizing will profit those who attend to it, not in the tongue but in the judgment. And one must, I think, who cares for truth, not compose his phrasing by design and pains, but try only to name, as he can, what he wishes. For from those who cling to the phrases and busy themselves about these, the matters slip away. It belongs to the husbandman to take, unharmed, the rose that grows among thorns, and to the craftsman to find out the pearl buried in the flesh of the oyster. And they say that birds too have the most pleasant quality of flesh when, no plentiful food being set before them, they themselves, scratching with their feet, pick out their food with toil. So if anyone, a contemplator of the like, longs that the true should be found, hidden among the many plausible and Greek things — as the true face beneath the masks — he will hunt it down by busying himself. For the power that appeared to Hermas in the vision says: "Whatever can be revealed to you will be revealed."

2.4. "And be not lifted up in your own wisdom," the Proverbs say, "but in all your ways make her known, that she may set straight your ways; and your foot shall not stumble." For by these things it wishes to show that the works must be in accordance with the word; but also that we must show that we have the useful, chosen out of all education. And the ways of wisdom are various that set straight toward the way of truth, and the way is faith. "And let not your foot stumble" — it speaks of certain things that seem to oppose the one and divine providential administration. Whence it adds: "Be not prudent in your own eyes" — according to the godless reasonings that set themselves against the dispensation of God — "but fear the only powerful God," upon which it follows that nothing is opposed to God. And besides, the addition teaches plainly that the divine fear is a turning away from evil; for it says: "And turn away from every evil." This is the discipline of wisdom; "for whom the Lord loves he disciplines," making him grieve unto understanding, but restoring him to peace and incorruption.

2.5. The barbarian philosophy, then, which we follow, is in truth perfect and true. So it says in Wisdom: "For he himself gave me an unerring knowledge of the things that are, to know the constitution of the world," and the rest, down to "and the powers of roots." In all these it has comprehended the natural contemplation, that concerning the world of sense, of all the things that have come to be. And next it hints also at the intelligible things, by what it adds: "And whatever is hidden and manifest I came to know; for wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me." You have, in brief, the promise of our philosophy. And the learning of these things, practised together with right conduct of life, leads up, through the wisdom that is the artificer of all things, to the Ruler of the universe — a thing hard to catch and hard to hunt, ever retreating and standing far off from the pursuer. Yet the same, being far off, has come very near — an unspeakable wonder. "I am a God who draws near," says the Lord — far off in essence (for how could the generated ever come near the ungenerated?), but very near in power, by which all things are enfolded in his bosom. "If anyone does anything in secret," he says, "shall I not see him?" And indeed the power of God is ever present, touching us by the power that beholds and benefits and educates.

2.6. Hence Moses, persuaded that God would never be known by human wisdom, says: "Show me yourself," and forces his way into the darkness where the voice of God was — that is, into the unapproachable and formless conceptions concerning Being. For God is not in darkness or in a place, but above both place and time and the property of the things that have come to be. Wherefore he is never found in a part, neither containing nor contained, either by some limit or by cutting off. "For what kind of house will you build me?" says the Lord. But he did not build even for himself, being uncontainable; and though heaven be called his throne, not even so is he contained, but he rests, delighting in his creation. It is plain, then, that the truth has been hidden from us — which has already been shown from one example, and a little later we shall present it through more.

2.7. And how are they not worthy of acceptance, both those who wish to learn and those who are able, according to Solomon, "to know wisdom and discipline, and to understand words of prudence, and to receive turnings of words, and to understand true righteousness" (as though there were also another not taught according to the truth, by the laws of the Greeks and the other philosophers) "and to set judgments straight" — not the judicial, but he indicates that we must have the criterion within us sound and unwandering — "that he may give to the harmless cunning, and to the young child perception and notion." For having heard these things, the wise man — the one persuaded to obey the commandments — will be wiser in knowledge, "and the man of understanding will gain guidance, and will understand a parable and a dark saying, the words of the wise and riddles." For the discourses inspired from God are not counterfeit, nor are those who traffic from them, nor yet are they snares, with which the many of the sophists entangle the young, busying themselves about nothing true. Rather, those who possess the Holy Spirit "search the depths of God" — that is, they become partakers of the hidden meaning concerning the prophecies. But to give the holy things to the dogs is forbidden, so long as they remain beasts; for it is never fitting to pour out for the envious and disturbed and still unbelieving characters, shameless in their barking inquiry, the divine and pure stream, the living water.

2.8. "Let not waters overflow for you outside your spring, but let your waters pass through into your streets." "For the many do not understand such things as they meet with, nor, having learned, do they know them, but seem so to themselves," according to the noble Heraclitus. Does it not seem to you that he too blames those who do not believe? "But my just man shall live by faith," the prophet has said. And another prophet too says: "Unless you believe, neither will you understand." For how could the soul ever hold the contemplation of these things, surpassing nature, with the unbelief about learning fighting within? But faith — which the Greeks slander, reckoning it empty and barbarian — is a voluntary anticipation, an assent of godliness, "the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen," according to the divine Apostle; "for by this especially the elders were witnessed to." And "without faith it is impossible to please God."

2.9. And others have rendered faith to be an assent of the mind to an unseen matter, just as, of course, demonstration is a manifest assent to a matter that was unknown. If, then, faith is a choice, being a kind of appetite for something, the appetite is here intellectual; and since choice is the beginning of action, faith is found to be the beginning of action, the foundation of an intelligent choice, when someone demonstrates beforehand to a man, through faith, the demonstration. And to follow willingly what is advantageous is the beginning of understanding. So an undistracted choice gives a great inclination toward knowledge. Indeed, the practice of faith becomes knowledge, propped upon a firm foundation. For the sons of the philosophers define knowledge as a state not to be shaken by reason. Is there, then, any other such state of true godliness itself, of which the Word alone is the teacher? I think not. And Theophrastus says that perception is the beginning of faith; for from this the beginnings extend toward the reason in us and the understanding. He, then, who has believed the divine Scriptures, having a firm judgment, receives as an irrefutable demonstration the voice of God who has granted the Scriptures. So faith is no longer fortified by demonstration. "Blessed, then, are those who have not seen and yet have believed." For the enchantments of the Sirens, displaying a superhuman power, astounded those who came near them, making them ready, almost against their will, for the reception of what was said.

3.10. Here those about Basilides hold faith to be natural, in which sense they also set it down under the head of election, as finding the studies without demonstration by an intellectual apprehension. But those from Valentinus, assigning faith to us, the simple, but knowledge to themselves, wish it to be inherent, by the advantage of a superior seed, in those who are saved by nature — knowledge far separated from faith, as they say the spiritual is from the natural. Further, those from Basilides say that faith, together with election, is proper to each interval; and that, as a consequence of the supramundane election, the worldly faith of every nature follows, and that the gift of faith is correspondent to the hope of each.

3.11. So faith is no longer a right achievement of choice, if it is an advantage of nature; nor will he who has not believed, being without responsibility, meet with a just recompense, nor he who has believed be responsible; and the whole property and difference of faith and unbelief would fall under neither praise nor blame, for those who reckon rightly, since it has, as its primary cause, a natural necessity that has come from the One who is able to do all things. And, we being drawn like puppets, after the manner of lifeless things, by natural activities, the voluntary and the involuntary are dragged along, and the impulse that leads these. And I, for one, no longer conceive of this as a living being, whose impulse has been allotted necessity, moved by a cause from outside. And where, any more, is the repentance of the once unbelieving, through which is the forgiveness of sins? So that neither is baptism any longer reasonable, nor the blessed seal, nor the Son, nor the Father; but God, I think, is found by them to be the distribution of natures, not having the foundation of salvation, the voluntary faith.

4.12. But we, who have received, through the Scriptures, that choice and avoidance have been given to men with a self-determining authority from the Lord, let us rest upon faith as an unwavering criterion, having shown the spirit ready, in that we have chosen life and have believed God through his voice. And he who has believed the Word knows the matter to be true; for the Word is truth. But he who has disbelieved the one who speaks has disbelieved God. "By faith we understand that the ages were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not come from things that appear," says the Apostle. "By faith Abel offered a fuller sacrifice than Cain, through which he was witnessed to be just, God bearing witness over his gifts; and through it, having died, he yet speaks" — and the rest, down to "than to have the temporary enjoyment of sin." These, then, even before the Law, faith justified and made heirs of the divine promise.

4.13. Why, then, should I still set out testimonies of faith, gathering them from the history among us? For the time would fail me to recount Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, and David and Samuel and the prophets, and what follows upon these. And of the four things in which the true resides — perception, mind, knowledge, assumption — by nature the mind is first, but to us and in relation to us perception is first; and out of perception and mind is constituted the essence of knowledge, and the evident is common to mind and perception. But perception is a stepping-stone of knowledge, while faith, having journeyed through the things of sense, leaves behind assumption, and hastens toward the unerring things and abides in the truth. And if anyone should say that knowledge is demonstrative with reason, let him hear that the first principles too are indemonstrable; for they are known neither by art nor by prudence. For the one is concerned with things that can be otherwise, and the other is productive only, not also contemplative.

4.14. By faith alone, then, is it possible to reach the principle of the universe. For all knowledge is teachable; and the teachable is from what is foreknown. But the principle of the universe was not foreknown to the Greeks — neither to Thales, who took water for the first cause, nor to the other natural philosophers in succession; since even if Anaxagoras first set mind over things, yet not even he preserved the efficient cause, depicting certain senseless whirls together with the inactivity and senselessness of mind. Wherefore the Word says: "Call no one your teacher upon the earth." For knowledge is a demonstrative state, but faith is a grace that brings up, from the indemonstrable, to the universal the simple — which is neither with matter, nor matter, nor under matter.

4.15. But the unbelievers, as it seems, drag all things down from heaven and the invisible to earth, "simply grasping rocks and oaks with their hands," according to Plato. For laying hold of all such things, they affirm that this alone is, which offers some collision and contact, defining body and essence as the same. But those who dispute against them defend themselves very cautiously from above, from some invisible quarter, contending that certain intelligible and incorporeal forms are the true essence. "Behold, I make new things," says the Word, "which eye has not seen nor ear heard nor has come up upon the heart of man" — with a new eye, a new hearing, a new heart, all that is visible and audible and apprehensible through faith and understanding, the disciples of the Lord speaking, hearing, doing spiritually. For there is an approved coin and another counterfeit, which deceives the laymen no less, but not the money-changers, who know, having learned, to separate and distinguish the counterfeit from the approved. So the money-changer says to the layman only this of the coin, that it is counterfeit; but the how, the why, only the banker's familiar and the one trained for this learns. And Aristotle says that the judgment that follows upon knowledge — that this thing is true — is faith. Faith, then, is more authoritative than knowledge and is its criterion.

4.16. And conjecture counterfeits faith, being a weak assumption, as the flatterer counterfeits the friend and the wolf the dog. But since we see that the carpenter, having learned, becomes a craftsman, and the pilot, educated in the art, will be able to steer — reckoning that to wish to become noble and good is not enough — it is necessary, then, being persuaded, to learn. And to be persuaded by the Word, whom we proclaimed teacher, is to believe in him in nothing opposing. For how is it possible to set oneself against God? Faithful, then, is knowledge, and knowable is faith, by a certain divine sequence and reciprocal sequence. Indeed, even Epicurus, who especially preferred pleasure to truth, supposes faith to be an anticipation of the mind; and he renders anticipation an application to something evident and to the evident conception of the thing; and that no one can either inquire or be at a loss, or even form an opinion, nor indeed refute, without an anticipation.

4.17. And how could anyone, not having an anticipation of what he reaches after, learn about what he inquires into? And he who has learned makes the anticipation already an apprehension. And if the learner does not learn without an anticipation receptive of the things said, he himself has ears that can hear the truth. And "blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who hear"; just as, of course, blessed is also he himself, of his obedience. And to hearken is to understand. If, then, faith is nothing other than an anticipation of the mind concerning the things said, and this is called both obedience and understanding and persuasion, no one will learn without faith, since neither without anticipation. And, being true beyond anything, that is demonstrated which was said by the prophet: "Unless you believe, neither will you understand." This too Heraclitus of Ephesus, paraphrasing the oracle, has said: "Unless he hope for the unhoped-for, he will not find it out, it being unsearchable and without passage."

4.18. But Plato the philosopher too, in the Laws, says that the man who is to become blessed and happy must, from the very beginning, be a partaker of the truth, that he may live as long a time as possible being true; for he is faithful. But the unfaithful is he to whom voluntary falsehood is dear; and he to whom it is involuntary is without sense; and neither of these is to be envied. For everyone who is unfaithful and unlearned is without a friend. And perhaps it is this that he calls, in a hidden way, the "kingly wisdom" in the Euthydemus. So in the Statesman he says, word for word: "So that the science of the true king is kingly, and he who possesses it, whether he be a ruler or a private man, will, at all events, according to the art itself, be rightly called kingly." So those who have believed in Christ both are and are called good (chrestoi), as those who are truly kingly are those cared for by a king. For as the wise are wise by wisdom, and the lawful lawful by law, so by Christ the king the Christians, the kingly ones of Christ. Then, going on, he adds clearly: "The right would be lawful, and law, being by nature, is right reason, and not in writings nor in other things." And the Eleatic stranger declares the kingly and statesmanlike man a living law.

4.19. And such is he who fulfils the law and does the will of the Father, but is plainly inscribed upon a certain lofty wood, set forth as an example of divine virtue to those able to discern. And the Greeks know the dispatch-staves of the ephors in Lacedaemon, on which the law was inscribed on wood; but my law, as has been said, is both kingly and living, and is right reason: "Law, the king of all, both mortals and immortals," as the Boeotian Pindar sings. For Speusippus, in the first book against Cleophon, seems to write the like to Plato through this: "For if kingship is a serious thing, and the wise man alone is king and ruler, then the law, being right reason, is serious" — which it indeed is. With these the Stoic philosophers dogmatize in agreement, attaching kingship, priesthood, prophecy, legislation, wealth, true beauty, nobility, and freedom to the wise man alone — who, however, is very exceedingly hard to find, as is confessed even by them.

5.20. All the aforesaid doctrines, then, appear to have been handed down to the Greeks from Moses the great. That all things belong to the wise man, he teaches through these: "And because God has had mercy on me, I have all things." And he shows him to be dear to God, saying: "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob." For the one is found called outright a friend, and the other is shown renamed as one who sees God; and Isaac, allegorized as a consecrated victim, he chose out for himself as a type to be for us of the saving dispensation. And among the Greeks too Minos is sung as "the nine-year king, the familiar of Zeus," they having heard how God conversed with Moses "as if one were to speak to his own friend."

5.21. Moses, then, was wise, king, legislator; but our Saviour surpasses all human nature. He is beautiful, so as to be loved by us alone who long for the true beauty, for he was "the true light"; and king he is shown to be, proclaimed both by children still untaught and by Jews unbelieving and ignorant, and heralded by the prophets themselves; and rich to such a degree that he disdained all the gold above and below the earth, together with all the glory, given to him by the adversary. Why need it be said that he alone is high priest, the only one who knows the service of God, the king of peace, Melchizedek, the most competent of all to lead the race of men? And legislator, in that he gives the law in the mouth of the prophets, most clearly enjoining and teaching what is to be done and what not.

5.22. And who could be of nobler birth than he, whose only father is God? Come, let us present Plato too, lighting upon the same doctrines. He has called the wise man rich in the Phaedrus, saying: "O dear Pan, and whatever other gods are here, grant me to become beautiful within; and as for what I have without, let it be friendly to what is within. And may I count the wise man rich." And the Athenian stranger, blaming those who think that the rich are those who have acquired much money, says thus: "But that those should be both very rich and good is impossible — those, that is, whom the many reckon rich; and they call rich those who have, among few of mankind, possessions worth the most money, which even a bad man may have acquired." "To the faithful belongs the whole world of riches," says Solomon, "but to the unfaithful not even an obol." Much more, then, must we be persuaded by the Scripture which says that a camel will pass through the eye of a needle sooner than a rich man philosophize; and, on the contrary, it blesses the poor, as Plato understood, saying: "Poverty is to be reckoned not the making of one's substance less, but the making of one's insatiability more. For it is never the smallness of property, but insatiability, from which the good man, being free, would also be rich." And in the Alcibiades he calls vice slavish, and virtue freeman-like. "Take from yourselves the heavy yoke," it says, "and take the gentle one," says the Scripture, just as the poets too call a yoke "slavish." And the "You were sold for your sins" agrees with what was said before. "Everyone, then, who does sin is a slave; and the slave does not abide in the house forever. But if the Son frees you, you will be free," and "the truth will free you." And again, that the wise man is beautiful, the Athenian says thus: "As if one should affirm that the just, even if they happen to be ugly in their bodies, are, by their most just character, in this respect altogether beautiful — scarcely would anyone speaking thus seem to speak amiss." And "his form was failing beyond all the sons of men," the prophecy foretold. And Plato has called the wise man king, in the Statesman, and the passage lies before us.

5.23. These things, then, being shown, let us run back again to the discourse concerning faith. Indeed, with all demonstration Plato presents that there is everywhere need of faith, somewhat thus, while at the same time hymning peace: "For a man faithful and sound in factions could not come to be without the whole of virtue. But of the mercenaries there are very many who are warlike and willing to die in war, of whom most become rash and unjust, insolent and senseless, except, indeed, some very few. If, then, these things are rightly said, every legislator who is of even small use will lay down his laws looking above all to the greatest virtue. And this is faithfulness, of which we have need at every time, both in peace and in every war and in the whole of the rest of life. For it seems, having gathered them, to contain the others." And the best is neither war nor faction; for it is to be deprecated to have need of these; but peace toward one another, and at the same time kindliness, is the strongest. From these it appears that the greatest prayer is to have peace, according to Plato, and that the greatest mother of the virtues is faith.

5.24. With reason, then, it is said in Solomon, "wisdom is in the mouth of the faithful," since Xenocrates too, in his work On Prudence, says that wisdom is the knowledge of the first causes and of the intelligible essence, holding prudence to be twofold, the one practical, the other contemplative, which last is human wisdom. Wherefore wisdom is prudence, but not all prudence is wisdom. And it has been shown that the knowledge of the principle of the universe is faith, but not demonstration. For it is absurd that the emulators of Pythagoras of Samos, declining the demonstrations of the things inquired into, should hold the "He himself said it" to be faith, and be content with this voice alone for the confirmation of what they have heard; but that the lovers of beholding the truth, undertaking to disbelieve a trustworthy teacher, the only Saviour God, should demand from him tests of what is said. But "he that has ears to hear, let him hear," he says. And who is this? Let Epicharmus tell: "Mind sees and mind hears; the rest is deaf and blind." That some are unbelieving Heraclitus says, rebuking them: "Not knowing how to hear or how to speak" — helped, no doubt, by Solomon: "If you love to hear, you will receive; and if you incline your ear, you will be wise."

6.25. "Lord, who has believed our report?" says Isaiah. "For faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of God," says the Apostle. "How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without one preaching? And how will they preach, unless they are sent? As it is written: 'How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good tidings of good things.'" You see how he brings faith up, through hearing and the preaching of the apostles, to the word of the Lord and the Son of God? Do we not yet understand that the word of the Lord is a demonstration? Just as playing at ball does not depend only on the one who, by skill, sends the ball, but also needs the one who receives it gracefully, that the exercise may be carried out according to the rules of ball-play, so it has come about that teaching too is trustworthy, when the faith of the hearers — being, so to speak, a kind of natural art — contributes toward the learning.

6.26. So earth too, being fruitful, works together toward the casting in of the seeds. For there is no use in the best education without the receiving of the learner, nor indeed of prophecy, when the ready obedience of the hearers is not present. For the dry chips, being ready to receive the burning power, are the more easily kindled; and the much-talked-of stone draws iron through kinship, as the amber too attracts chips and the electron stirs up bits of chaff; and the things drawn obey them, drawn by an unspeakable breath, not as causes but as joint causes. Vice, then, being twofold in kind — the one leading on with deceit and by stealth, the other forcing and carrying off — the divine Word has cried out, calling all together, knowing well, indeed, even those who will not be persuaded; yet, since it lies with us to be persuaded or not, that none may have ignorance to plead, it has made the calling just, and demands from each according to his power. For to some, together with the willing, the being able is present, who have increased this by exercise and are cleansed; and others, even if they cannot yet, already have the willing. And to will is the work of the soul, but to do is not without the body. Nor are matters measured by the end alone, but are judged also by each man's choice — whether he chose readily, whether he repented of the things in which he sinned, whether he gained understanding of the things in which he stumbled, and changed his mind, which is to know afterward; for repentance is a slow knowing, but the first knowledge is sinlessness.

6.27. Repentance, then, is also a right achievement of faith. For unless one believes that what he was held by before is a sin, he will not change; and unless he believes that punishment hangs over the offender, but salvation over the one who lives according to the commandments, he will not, even so, change. And hope too is composed of faith. So those from Basilides define faith as an assent of the soul to something of those things that do not move the perception because they are not present. And hope is the expectation of the acquisition of a good; and the expectation must be faithful. And faithful is he who keeps inviolably the things entrusted; and there are entrusted to us the discourses concerning God and the divine words, the commandments, together with the carrying out of the precepts. This is the faithful servant, the one praised by the Lord. And when one says "God is faithful," he indicates that one ought to believe him when he declares; and his Word declares, and God himself would be faithful. How, then, if to believe is to suppose, do the philosophers think the things from them firm? For an assumption is not a voluntary assent before demonstration, but an assent to something strong.

6.28. And who would be stronger than God? But unbelief is a weak, negative assumption of the opposite, just as distrust is a state hard to receive faith. And faith is a voluntary assumption and a kindly anticipation before apprehension, and an expectation of what is to come; while the expectation of other things is an opinion of the uncertain; and confidence is a firm conviction about something. Wherefore we believe in him in whom we have placed confidence, unto divine glory and salvation; and we have placed confidence in the only God, whom we know that he will not transgress the things well promised to us, and made and granted to us by him out of goodwill. And goodwill is the willing of good things for another for that one's own sake. For the one is without need; but to us the beneficence and the favour from the Lord come down, being divine goodwill, and goodwill that is toward doing good. And if to Abraham, believing, it was reckoned for righteousness, and we are the seed of Abraham through hearing, then we too must believe. For we are Israelites who are obedient not through signs, but through hearing. "Therefore be glad, you barren one who do not bear; break forth and cry," it says, "you who do not travail; for many are the children of the desolate, more than of her who has the husband." "You lived within the enclosure of the people; your children were blessed into the tents of the fathers." And if the same dwellings are announced by prophecy to us and to the patriarchs, one God is shown for both covenants.

6.29. So it adds more clearly: "You have inherited the covenant of Israel" — speaking to the calling from the nations, once barren of this husband, who is the Word, once desolate of the bridegroom. "But the just shall live by faith" — the faith according to the covenant and the commandments — since these two, in name and in time, given according to age and advance dispensationally, being in power one, the one old, the other new, are supplied through the Son from one God. So the Apostle too, in the Epistle to the Romans, says: "For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith" — teaching the one salvation, perfected from prophecy into the Gospel through one and the same Lord. "This charge I commit to you, child Timothy, according to the prophecies that went before upon you, that you may war in them the good warfare, having faith and a good conscience, which some, having thrust away, have made shipwreck concerning the faith," because they defiled with unbelief the conscience that came from God.

6.30. With reason, then, faith is no longer to be slandered as ready-to-hand, easy, and common, and besides of chance people. For if it were a human pursuit, as the Greeks supposed, it would have been quenched; but it grows, and there is no place where it is not. I say, then, that faith — whether it was founded by love or even by fear, as the accusers say — is something divine, neither torn apart by another worldly friendship nor dissolved by fear when present. For love makes the faithful by the friendship that is toward faith; and faith, the seat of love, brings in beneficence in return, when even the schoolmaster fear of the law is believed in by those who believe. And it is believed that fear too is; for if in acting the being is shown, then he who is to come and threatens, but does not act or come present, is believed even to be; and, being believed to be, he is not himself the begetter of faith, being judged trustworthy by it.

6.31. Divine, then, is so great a change, that one becomes faithful out of unfaithful and believes by hope and by fear. And indeed the first inclination toward salvation appears to us as faith, after which fear and hope and repentance, together with self-control and endurance, advancing, lead us on both to love and to knowledge. With reason, then, the Apostle Barnabas says: "From what I received I was eager to send to you a part, little by little, that together with your faith you might have also perfect knowledge." "The helpers of our faith, then, are fear and endurance; and the things that fight with us are long-suffering and self-control. While these," he says, "abide in purity toward the Lord, there rejoice together with them wisdom, understanding, science, knowledge." Since, then, knowledge has as its elements the aforesaid virtues, it has come about that faith is more elementary still — being as necessary to the gnostic as breathing is to living for the one who lives in this world; and as without the four elements it is not possible to live, so without faith it is not possible for knowledge to follow. This, then, is the foundation of truth.

7.32. But those who accuse fear run down the law; and if the law, then plainly the God too who gave the law. For these three things necessarily exist about the subject matter: the administrator, the administration, the thing administered. If, then, by hypothesis they should take away the law, then necessarily each man who is led by desire, gratifying pleasure, will neglect what is good, despise the divine, and be at once impious and unjust, leaping away fearlessly from the truth. "Yes," they say, "fear is an irrational avoidance and a passion." What do you say? And how could this definition still hold for you, the commandment having been given me through reason? And the commandment forbids, hanging fear over us, for the education of those who can thus be admonished. Fear, then, is not irrational, but rather rational; for how is it not, when it advises, "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness"? But if they quibble about the names, let the philosophers call the fear of the law "caution."

7.33. As being a reasonable avoidance. These men Critolaus of Phaselis, not amiss, called "word-fighters." Already, then, the commandment has appeared elegant and most noble to those who accuse us, when understood by a change of name. Caution, then, is shown to be rational, being an avoidance of what harms, from which springs the repentance of former sins. "For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and good understanding is to all who do it." He calls "doing" of wisdom that which is the fear of God paving the way to wisdom. And if the law is productive of fear, the beginning of wisdom is the knowledge of the law, and there is no wise man without law. Without sense, then, are those who decline the law, upon which it follows that they are reckoned godless. "And education is the beginning of wisdom. But the impious will despise wisdom and education," says the Scripture.

7.34. Let us see what fearful things the law announces. If they are the things between virtue and vice — such as poverty and disease and ill repute and low birth, and the like — these the laws of the city too are praised for setting forth; and to the men of the Peripatos, who introduce three kinds of goods and reckon their opposites to be evils, this opinion is harmonious. But to us the given law commands to flee the things that are truly evil — adultery, lasciviousness, pederasty, ignorance, injustice, disease of soul, death — not the death that dissolves soul from body, but that which dissolves soul from truth; for these vices and the activities from them are truly terrible and fearful. "Not unjustly are nets stretched out for the winged," say the divine oracles; "for they themselves, sharing in blood, treasure up evils for themselves." How, then, is the law any longer said not to be good, by certain heresies that cry out the Apostle's saying, "for through the law is knowledge of sin"? To whom we say: the law did not make, but showed, the sin; for, having commanded what is to be done, it convicted what is not to be done. And it belongs to the good both to teach the saving thing and to point out the poisonous, and to counsel the use of the one and command the avoiding of the other.

7.35. So the Apostle, whom they do not understand, said that knowledge of sin was made manifest through the law, not that it received its existence. And how is the law that educates not good, the schoolmaster given for Christ, that we may turn, being directed by fear in educative fashion toward the perfecting that is through Christ? "I do not wish the death of the sinner," he says, "so much as his repentance." And the commandment makes repentance, being preventive of the things not to be done, and promising the beneficences. By "death," I think, he means ignorance. And "he who is near the Lord is full of scourges" — that is, he who draws near to knowledge enjoys dangers, fears, griefs, afflictions, on account of the longing for the truth. "For an educated son turned out wise, and a son of understanding was saved from burning; and a son of understanding will receive commandments." And Barnabas the Apostle, having set first, "Woe to those who are prudent in themselves and knowing in their own eyes," added: "Let us become spiritual, a perfect temple to God. As far as is in us, let us practise the fear of God and strive to keep his commandments, that we may rejoice in his ordinances." Whence "the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom" is divinely said.

8.36. Here those about Basilides, expounding this saying, say that the Archon himself, hearing the utterance of the ministering Spirit, was struck with astonishment both at the hearing and at the sight, having beyond hope received good tidings; and that his astonishment was called fear, becoming the beginning of a wisdom that distinguishes by classes, and discerns, and perfects, and restores. For not only the world, but also the election, the One over all, having distinguished, sends forth. And Valentinus too, in a certain letter, seems to have had such things in mind, writing in these very words: "And as though there came to be fear upon that creature among the angels, when it spoke greater things than its formation, on account of the one who had invisibly given in it a seed of the essence from above and who spoke with frankness; so too in the generations of worldly men the works of men became fears to those who made them — such as statues and images and all that hands accomplish in the name of God. For Adam, formed in the name of Man, gave fear of the pre-existing Man, as though he himself stood in him; and they were astounded, and quickly made the work vanish."

8.37. But there being one principle, as will be shown later, these men will appear to be inventing twitterings and warblings. And since it seemed good to God that men should be educated beforehand, through the Lord, from the law and the prophets, "the fear of the Lord is said to be the beginning of wisdom" — given by the Lord through Moses to the disobedient and hard-hearted; for those whom reason does not take, fear tames. Which the educating Word too, foreseeing from above, fitted as an instrument, in each of the two ways, cleansing fittingly toward godliness. Astonishment, then, is a fear from an unaccustomed impression, or at an unexpected impression — as also of a message; and fear is as at something that has come to be or is, or an excessive marvelling. They do not, then, perceive that they make passible, through astonishment, the greatest God, the one hymned even by them, and one who, before the astonishment, came to be in ignorance. And if ignorance preceded the astonishment, and the astonishment and the fear became the beginning of the wisdom of God, then ignorance is in danger of preceding causally the wisdom of God and the whole world-making, and indeed the restoration of the election itself.

8.38. Is the ignorance, then, of good things or of base? But if of good things, why does it cease at astonishment? And the minister is superfluous to them, and the proclamation and the baptism. But if of base things, how is the evil the cause of the noblest things? For unless ignorance had pre-existed, the minister would not have come down, nor would astonishment have taken the Archon, as they themselves say, nor would he have received a beginning of wisdom from the fear, for the distinguishing of the election and of the worldly things. And if the fear of the pre-existing Man made the angels plotters against their own creature — as though the seed of the essence from above were invisibly seated in the work — either by an empty supposition they were jealous, which is implausible, that angels should become slayers of a creation entrusted to them, like some child, being condemned of all ignorance; or, held in foreknowledge, they were moved, but then they would not have plotted, through what they attempted, against him whom they foreknew, nor would they have been astounded at their own work, having from foreknowledge perceived the seed from above; or, lastly, trusting in knowledge, they dared — which is itself impossible, that those who had learned the superior thing in the Man of the Fullness should plot against it, and further against that according to the image, in which they had received both the archetype and the incorruptible together with the rest of the knowledge.

8.39. To these very men, then, and to certain others, but especially to those from Marcion, the Scripture cries out, though they do not hear: "But he who hears me shall rest in peace, trusting, and shall be at ease without fear from every evil." What, then, do they wish the law to be? Evil, indeed, they will not say, but just, distinguishing the good from the just. But the Lord, commanding to fear the evil, does not put away the evil by evil, but dissolves the contrary by the contrary. And evil is contrary to good, as just to unjust. If, then, he has called the abstinence from evils "fearlessness," which the fear of the Lord works, the fear is a good; and the fear from the law is not only just but also good, doing away with vice. And, by fear introducing fearlessness, not by passion impassivity, but by education it produces moderation of passion. When, then, we hear, "Honour the Lord, and you shall be strong; but besides him fear no other," we take it that to fear sinning, and to follow the commandments given by God, is the honour of God.

8.40. And dread is a fear of the divine. But even if fear is a passion, as some wish, because fear is a passion, not all fear is a passion. Superstition, at any rate, is a passion, being a fear of demons, both passion-ridden and passionate; but, on the contrary, the fear of the impassible God is impassible; for one fears not God, but the falling away from God; and he who dreads this — the falling into evils — fears and dreads the evils; and he who dreads the fall wishes himself to be incorruptible and impassible. "The wise man, fearing, turned away from evil; but the fool, trusting, mingles with it," says the Scripture; and again, "In the fear of the Lord is hope of strength," it says.

9.41. Such fear, then, leads up both to repentance and to hope. And hope is the expectation of good things, the good hope of an absent good. Indeed, even . . . readiness-to-fall is taken into hope, which we have learned to lead by the hand toward love. And love would be a concord of the things according to reason and life and manner — or, to speak briefly, a fellowship of life, or an intensity of friendship and tender affection, with right reason, about the use of a companion. And the companion is a second self; whence we call brothers those reborn by the same word. And beside love lie hospitality, being a kind of fond skill about the use of strangers; and strangers are those to whom worldly things are strange. For we understand as worldly those who hope toward earth and the fleshly desires. "Be not conformed," says the Apostle, "to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of the mind, that you may approve what is the will of God, the good and well-pleasing and perfect." Hospitality, then, busies itself about what is profitable to strangers; and strangers are guests, and guests are friends, and friends are brothers: "dear brother," says Homer. And love of mankind, through which is tender affection too, being a friendly use of men; and tender affection, being a kind of fond skill about the cherishing of friends or kindred, accompany love.

9.42. And if the true man in us is the spiritual, then love of mankind is brotherly love toward those who have shared the same spirit. And cherishing, again, is the keeping of goodwill or of fondness; and fondness is a complete acceptance, and to love is to be pleased with the character, being led toward and away. And men are led into sameness through concord, which is the science of common goods; for concord too is a harmony of judgments. And "let love be unfeigned among us," he says, "and let us ourselves, abhorring the evil, become joined to the good in brotherly love," and the rest, down to "if possible, as far as in you lies, being at peace with all men." Then he says, "Be not overcome by the evil, but overcome the evil in the good." And the same Apostle confesses to bear witness of the Jews that "they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge; for, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God." For they neither knew nor did the will of the law, but what they themselves supposed, this they thought the law too wished; nor did they believe the law as prophesying, but followed it by bare word and fear, not by disposition and faith. "For the end of the law is Christ unto righteousness" — the one prophesied by the law — "to everyone who believes."

9.43. Whence it is said to these by Moses: "I will provoke you to jealousy over what is no nation; over a nation without understanding I will anger you" — meaning, of course, the nation made ready for obedience. And through Isaiah he says: "I was found by those who did not seek me; I became manifest to those who did not ask after me" — before the coming of the Lord, that is; after which those prophesied things too are now fittingly said of Israel: "I stretched out my hands all the day to a disobedient and gainsaying people." You see the cause of the calling from the nations plainly stated by the prophet — the disobedience and gainsaying of the people? Then the goodness of God is shown even in these things; for the Apostle says: "But by their falling away salvation came to the nations, to provoke them to jealousy and to make them wish to repent." And the Shepherd, having put the saying simply about those who have fallen asleep, knows certain just men among the nations and among the Jews, not only before the coming of the Lord, but also before the law, according to their pleasing of God, like Abel, like Noah, like any other just man.

9.44. So he says that the apostles and teachers who preached the name of the Son of God and fell asleep, in power and faith, preached to those who had fallen asleep before. Then he adds: "And they themselves gave them the seal of the preaching. They went down, then, with them into the water, and again came up. But these went down living and again came up living; while those who had fallen asleep before went down dead and came up living. Through these, then, they were made alive and came to know the name of the Son of God. For this reason they also came up together with them and were fitted together into the building of the tower, and were built in unhewn; for they fell asleep in righteousness and in great purity, only this seal they had not." "For when the nations that do not have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves," according to the Apostle.

9.45. That the virtues follow one another reciprocally, what need is there to say, since it has already been shown that faith is upon repentance and hope, and caution upon faith, and that the abiding in these and the exercise, together with learning, are brought to completion in love, which in turn is perfected by knowledge? But this must of necessity be noted: that the divine alone must be conceived as wise by nature; wherefore wisdom too is the power of God that has taught the truth; and here, somewhere, the perfecting of knowledge has been taken. And the philosopher loves and is fond of the truth, being, from a genuine servant, already reckoned a friend through love. And the beginning of this is to wonder at the things that are, as Plato says in the Theaetetus, and as Matthias too, in the Traditions, advises: "Wonder at the things present," laying this down as the first step toward the knowledge beyond. So in the Gospel according to the Hebrews too it is written: "He who has wondered will reign, and he who has reigned will rest." It is impossible, then, for the unlearned, so long as he remains unlearned, to philosophize — at least the man who has not received a notion of wisdom, philosophy being a reaching after the truly existing and after the studies that tend toward this. And even if doing well is practised by some, yet the knowing how one must use and do must be worked out together, in respect of which one is also made like to God — to God, I mean, the Saviour — serving the God of the universe through the high-priestly Word, through whom are beheld the things that are truly noble and just. Reverence . . . is an action that follows and is consequent upon God.

10.46. Three things, then, does our own philosopher hold to: first, contemplation; second, the fulfilling of the commandments; third, the equipping of good men — which, coming together, complete the gnostic. And whatever of these is lacking, the things of knowledge go lame. Whence divinely the Scripture says: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: I am the Lord your God. According to the pursuits of the land of Egypt, in which you dwelt, you shall not do; and according to the pursuits of the land of Canaan, into which I bring you there, you shall not do; and in their customs you shall not walk. My judgments you shall do, and my ordinances you shall keep, to walk in them: I am the Lord your God. And you shall keep all my ordinances and do them. The man who does them shall live in them: I am the Lord your God."

10.47. Whether, then, Egypt and the land of Canaan are a symbol of the world and of deceit, or of passions and vices, from which one must abstain, and what things are to be practised as divine and not worldly, the oracle shows us. And when it says, "The man who does them shall live in them," it calls life both the correction of the Hebrews themselves and the joint-exercise and advance of those near, of our very selves. For "those dead in trespasses are made alive together with Christ" through our covenant. And the Scripture, often repeating "I am the Lord your God," most turningly puts us to shame, teaching us to follow the God who gave the commandments; and it gently reminds us to seek God and to attempt to know him so far as may be — which would be the greatest contemplation, the higher vision, the science in truth, that which comes to be unwavering by reason. This alone would be the knowledge of wisdom, from which right action is never separated.

11.48. But the knowledge of the reputed wise — whether they be barbarian heresies or the philosophers among the Greeks — "puffs up," according to the Apostle. But faithful is the knowledge which is a scientific demonstration of the things handed down according to the true philosophy. And we would say that it is a reasoning which furnishes faith for the things in dispute out of the things agreed upon. And faith being twofold, the one scientific, the other based on opinion, nothing hinders us from naming demonstration twofold, the one scientific, the other based on opinion — since knowledge too, and foreknowledge, are called twofold, the one having its own nature made exact, the other deficient. And surely the demonstration that is among us would alone be true, as being supplied from the divine Scriptures, the sacred writings, and the God-taught wisdom, according to the Apostle. Learning, at any rate, is also the obeying of the commandments, which is to believe God. And faith is a certain power of God, being a strength of the truth.

11.49. So it says: "If you have faith as a grain of mustard, you will remove the mountain"; and again, "According to your faith be it to you"; and the one is healed, having received the cure through his faith, and the other, who is dead, is raised through the strength of him who believed that he would rise. But the demonstration based on opinion is human, and comes from rhetorical arguments or dialectical syllogisms. For the highest demonstration, which we hinted to be scientific, sets faith in the souls of those who long to learn, through the setting-out and opening of the Scriptures — which would be knowledge. For if the things taken up toward the thing inquired are taken as true, as being divine and prophetic, it is plain that the conclusion drawn from them will, in consequence, be brought in as true; and rightly would knowledge be a demonstration for us.

11.50. So when the memorial of the heavenly and divine food was commanded to be consecrated in a golden jar, "the gomor," it says, "was the tenth of the three measures." For in us ourselves three measures, three criteria, are indicated: perception of things of sense; of things said, both names and words, reason; and of things of thought, mind. The gnostic, then, will abstain from the sins that are according to reason and according to thought and according to perception and activity, having heard how "he who looked toward desire committed adultery," and having taken to mind that "blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God," and knowing that too, that "not the things that enter into the mouth defile the man, but those that come out through the mouth, these defile the man; for out of the heart come the reasonings." This, I think, is the true and just measure according to God, by which the things measured are measured — the decad that holds the man together, which, in summary, the aforesaid three measures showed. And it would be body and soul, and the five senses, and the vocal power and the seminal, and the rational or spiritual — or however you wish to call it.

11.51. And one must, so to speak, mounting up above all the others, stand upon the mind — just as, indeed, in the world, having leaped over the nine portions, the first being that of the four elements set in one region because of their equal change, and then the seven wandering and the eighth unwandering — coming to the perfect number above the nine, the tenth portion, to arrive at the knowledge of God, longing, in a word, after the Maker, after the creation. For this reason the tithes both of the ephi and of the victims were brought to God, and the feast of the Passover began from the tenth, being a passing over from every passion and every thing of sense. The gnostic, then, is fixed in faith; but the man of conceited wisdom willingly does not touch the truth, using unstable and unsettled impulses. With reason, then, it is written: "And Cain went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Naid over against Eden"; and Naid is interpreted "tossing," Eden "delight." And faith and knowledge and peace are the delight, from which the man who disobeys is cast out; but the man of conceited wisdom from the beginning does not even wish to hear the divine commandments, but, like a self-taught one who has thrown off the rein, willingly removes into the surging tossing, going down to mortal and generated things from the knowledge of the ungenerated, holding now one opinion, now another. "And those who have no guidance fall like leaves." Reason and the governing part, remaining unstumbling and leading the soul, is called its pilot; for in truth the approach to the unchangeable is by the unchangeable.

11.52. So Abraham was "standing before the Lord, and, drawing near, said"; and to Moses it is said, "But you, stand here with me." But those about Simon wish to be made like in their manner to the "Standing One" whom they revere. Faith, then, and the knowledge of the truth ever make the soul that has chosen them to be in the same condition and after the same manner. But akin to falsehood are change and turning aside and departure, as to the gnostic belong stillness and rest and peace. As, then, conceit and self-opinion have slandered philosophy, so too false knowledge — called by the same name — has slandered knowledge; concerning which the Apostle, writing, says: "O Timothy, keep the deposit, turning away from the profane empty talkings and oppositions of the falsely-named knowledge, which some, professing, have missed the mark concerning the faith." Convicted by this saying, those from the heresies reject the Epistles to Timothy. Come, then: if the Lord is truth and wisdom and the power of God, as indeed he is, it would be shown that the man who has known him, and the Father through him, is in truth a gnostic; for he perceives along with the one who says: "The lips of the just know lofty things."

12.53. And faith, like time, being twofold, we would find two virtues dwelling with both. For of time, to the past belongs memory, to the future hope; and we believe that the past has come to be and that the future will be; and again we love, persuaded by faith that the past is so, and awaiting the future by hope. For through all things love has gone forth to the gnostic who knows one God; and, "behold, all things which he has made are very good," he knows and marvels at. And "godliness adds length of life, and the fear of the Lord adds days." As, then, the days are a portion of the life that is by ascent, so too fear is the beginning of love, becoming, by increase, faith, then love — but not as I fear the wild beast and hate it (fear being twofold), but as I dread the father too, whom I both fear and love at once. Again, fearing lest I be punished, I love myself, choosing the fear; but he who fears to offend the father loves him. Blessed, then, is he who becomes faithful, mingled of love and fear; for faith is strength unto salvation, and power unto eternal life.

12.54. Again, prophecy is foreknowledge, and knowledge is the understanding of prophecy — that is, knowledge of the things foreknown to those men by the Lord who makes all things plain beforehand. The knowledge of the things foretold, then, shows their issue to be threefold: either having come to pass long ago, or already present, or to be in the future. Then the extremes have fallen under faith — of things accomplished or of things hoped for; but the present activity furnishes conviction for the confirmation of both extremes. For if, prophecy being one, the one part is now accomplished and the other fulfilled, from this both the hoped-for is trustworthy and the past is true. For first it was present, then it has passed for us, so that the faith of past things is an apprehension of a past thing, and the hope of future things an apprehension of a future thing. And the assents — not only those from Plato, but also those from the Stoa — say are in our power.

12.55. Every opinion, then, and judgment and assumption and learning, by which we live and are ever in company with the race of men, is an assent; and this would be nothing other than faith. And unbelief too, being a departure from faith, shows assent and faith to be possible; for a privation of a non-existent thing could not be spoken of. And if anyone considers the truth, he will find man by nature ill-disposed toward assent to falsehood, but having occasions toward faith in the truth. The virtue that holds the Church together, as the Shepherd says, is faith, through which the elect of God are saved; and that which plays the man is self-control. And there follow upon these simplicity, knowledge, harmlessness, gravity, love. And all these are daughters of faith. And again: "Faith leads the way, fear builds up, and love perfects." "One must fear the Lord, then," he says, "unto building up, but not the devil unto overthrow." And, on the contrary: "the works of the Lord — that is, the commandments — must be loved and done, but the works of the devil feared and not done"; for the fear of God educates and restores to love, but the works of the devil have hatred as their housemate. And the same author says that repentance is great understanding; for he who repents of what he has done no longer does or says it, but, torturing his own soul for the things in which he sinned, works good. Forgiveness of sins, then, differs from repentance, but both show the things in our power.

13.56. He who has received the forgiveness of sins, then, must no longer sin. For upon the first and only repentance of sins (this would be of the sins that pre-existed in the gentile and first life, the one in ignorance, I mean) there is set forth at once, to those called, the repentance that cleanses the place of the soul from offences, that faith may be founded. And the Lord, being a knower of hearts and foreknowing the things to come, both the changeableness of man and the shiftiness and craftiness of the devil, foresaw from the very beginning above how the devil, being jealous over the forgiveness of the man's sins, would fasten certain causes of sins upon the servants of God, working evil prudently, that they too might fall away together with him.

13.57. He gave, then, yet another repentance, a second, to those who, even in the faith, fall into some offence, being very merciful, that, if anyone be tempted after the calling, but forced and over-reached by craft, he may receive still one repentance not to be repented of. For "if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there is no longer left a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and a zeal of fire that is about to devour the adversaries." But the continual and repeated repentances upon sins differ in nothing from those who have not believed at all, except only in the perceiving that they sin; and I do not know which of the two is worse — to sin knowingly, or, having repented of the sins, to offend again. For by either way the sin is shown by conviction: the one condemned at the doing by the worker of lawlessness, the other by the man who, foreknowing the thing to be done as base, attempts it. And the one perhaps gratifies anger and pleasure, not ignorant whom he gratifies; but the other, repenting of what he gratified, then running back again to pleasure, is joined to the one who from the beginning willingly sins; for he who does again that of which he repented, doing what he has condemned,

13.58. does it willingly. He, then, who from the nations and from that former life rushed to faith, once obtained forgiveness of sins; but he who, even after these things, has sinned, then repents, even if he meet with pardon, ought to be ashamed, no longer washing himself unto forgiveness of sins. For he must leave behind not only the idols which he formerly deified, but also the works of his former life — the man not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but reborn in spirit; which would be not to repent of the same offence into which he has been carried. For to repent often is, on the contrary, a practice of sins, and an aptitude toward readiness, from want of training.

13.59. To ask pardon often for the things in which we often offend is, then, a semblance of repentance, not repentance. "But righteousness cuts straight blameless ways," cries the Scripture. And again: "The righteousness of the harmless will set straight his way." Indeed, "as a father pities his sons, so the Lord pitied those who fear him," David writes. "Those, then, who sow in tears," of those who in repentance make confession, "will reap in gladness; for blessed are all who fear the Lord." You see the blessing that resembles those in the Gospel? "Fear not," it says, "when a man becomes rich, and when the glory of his house is multiplied; for in his dying he will not take all things, nor will his glory go down with him. But I, in your mercy, will enter into your house; I will worship toward your holy temple in your fear. Lord, lead me in your righteousness." Now impulse is a movement of the mind toward something or away from it; and passion is an excessive impulse, or one overstraining the measures according to reason, or an impulse carried away and disobedient to reason. So passions are a movement of the soul contrary to nature, in the disobedience toward reason. (And the departure and the standing-out and the disobedience are in our power, as obedience too is in our power; wherefore the voluntary things are judged.) And indeed if one should go through each of the passions one by one, one would find them irrational appetites.

14.60. The involuntary, then, is not judged (and this is twofold: the one coming about with ignorance, the other by necessity); for how could you give judgment about the things said to be sinned according to the involuntary modes? For either a man was ignorant of himself, as Cleomenes and Athamas who went mad; or of the thing he does, as Aeschylus, who, having uttered the mysteries on the stage, was judged in the Areopagus and so released, having shown himself not initiated; or one might be ignorant of the person about whom it is done, as the man who let go the adversary and killed his own instead of the enemy; or of that wherein it is done, as the man who, exercising with spears tipped with balls, and killing someone when the spear cast off its ball; or of the manner — as the man in the stadium who killed his antagonist (for he contended not for death but for victory); or of that for the sake of which it is done — as the physician who gave a wholesome antidote and killed, yet gave it not for this, but to save.

14.61. The law of that time held even the involuntary slayer, as it held the involuntary one with an issue, but not on a par with the voluntary. And yet he too will be punished as for a voluntary thing, if one transfer the passion to the truth; for in truth he is to be punished who cannot control the seminal reason. Which is itself an irrational passion of the soul, going near to babbling; but the faithful man has chosen to hide matters with discretion. The things of choice, then, are judged; "for the Lord searches hearts and reins"; and "he who looked toward desire is judged." Wherefore "You shall not even desire," it says; and "This people honours me with the lips," it says, "but their heart is far from me." For God looks to the very judgment, since he left Lot's wife too, who turned, willingly only, toward the worldly vice, without perception, having shown her as a pillar of salt and fixed her so as not to advance — not a foolish and useless image, but one to season and to give pungency to the man able to discern spiritually.

15.62. And the voluntary is either according to appetite, or according to choice, or according to thought. So these stand somehow beside one another: error, mishap, wrongdoing. And there is error — say, to live luxuriously and licentiously; mishap — to strike a friend as an enemy through ignorance; and wrongdoing — grave-robbing or sacrilege. And erring is constituted from not knowing how to judge what one must do, or from being unable to do it; just as, indeed, a man falls into a pit either through ignorance or through being unable to leap over it because of weakness of body. But in our power, at all events, are both our standing toward our education and our obedience toward the commandments.

15.63. And if we should not wish to share in these, giving ourselves over to anger and desire, we shall err, or rather we shall wrong our own soul. For that Laius in the tragedy says: "None of these things of which you admonish me has escaped me; yet, though I have judgment, nature forces me" — that is, his having become given over to the passion. And Medea too likewise cries out on the stage: "And I understand what evils I am about to do, but my anger is stronger than my counsels." Nor is Ajax silent, but, about to slay himself, cries out: "No grief so gnaws the soul of a free man as dishonour. So have I suffered, and a deep stain, welling up from the depths, turns me back, goaded with the bitter spurs of madness."

15.64. These, then, anger sets in tragedy; but desire, ten thousand others — Phaedra, Antheia, Eriphyle, "who received precious gold for her dear husband." For that comic Thrasonides, another stage says: "A cheap little slave-girl has enslaved me." Mishap, then, is an error contrary to reason; and error is an involuntary wrongdoing, but wrongdoing a voluntary vice. Error, then, is mine, involuntary. Wherefore he says: "For sin shall not have lordship over you; for you are not under law but under grace" — speaking to those who have already believed, that "by his stripe we were healed." And misfortune is an involuntary action of another upon me; but wrongdoing alone is found voluntary, whether mine or another's.

15.65. These differences of sins the Psalmist hints at, calling blessed those whose lawlessnesses God has wiped out, and whose sins he has covered, and the others he has not reckoned, and the rest he has forgiven. For it is written: "Blessed are those whose lawlessnesses are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not reckon sin, nor is there guile in his mouth." This blessing came upon those chosen by God through Jesus Christ our Lord. For love covers a multitude of sins; but he wipes them out who chooses the repentance of the sinner rather than his death.

15.66. And those sins are not reckoned which are not constituted according to choice; for "he who desired has already committed adultery," it says. And the enlightening Word forgives sins; and "in that time," says the Lord, "they will seek the iniquity of Israel, and it shall not be, and the sins of Judah, and they shall not be found; for who is like me? And who shall stand against my face?" You see one God announced, good, both apportioning according to worth and forgiving sins. And John too, in the greater Epistle, plainly teaches the differences of sins in these words: "If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin not unto death, he shall ask, and he will give him life" — speaking of those who sin not unto death; "for there is a sin unto death; not concerning that do I say that anyone should ask." "All unrighteousness is sin,"

15.67. and there is a sin not unto death. But David too, and before David Moses, show forth the knowledge of the three doctrines in these words: "Blessed is the man who walked not in the counsel of the impious" — as the fishes go in darkness into the depths; for those that have no scales, which Moses forbids to touch, feed at the bottom of the sea — "nor stood in the way of sinners" — as those who seem to fear the Lord sin like the pig; for, when hungry, it cries out, but when filled does not recognize its master — "nor sat in the seat of the pestilent" — as the winged creatures ready for plunder. And Moses advised: "You shall not eat the pig, nor the eagle, nor the sharp-winged, nor the raven, nor any fish that has not a scale in itself." This is from Barnabas. But I, for one, have heard a wise man interpret such things, saying that the "counsel of the impious" is the nations, and taking the "way of sinners" to be the Jewish supposition, and the "seat of the pestilent" the heresies.

15.68. But another said, more authoritatively, that the first blessing is set upon those who did not follow after the wicked judgments — those that apostatized from God; the second upon those who do not abide in the broad and wide way — whether those reared in the law, or those from the nations who have repented; and the "seat of the pestilent" would be the theatres and the law-courts; or, rather, the following after the wicked and ruinous authorities, and the fellowship in their works. "But his will is in the law of the Lord" — Peter, in the Preaching, called the Lord both law and Word. And the legislator seems, in another way too, to teach the abstinence from sin in three modes: from those in word, through the voiceless fishes (for there is in truth a place where silence is better than word; there is also a guerdon of silence, free of danger); from those in deed, through the rapacious and flesh-eating birds; . . . the pig delights in mire and dung;

15.69. and one must not even have the conscience defiled. With reason, then, the prophet says: "Not so the impious, not so, but as the chaff which the wind drives from the face of the earth. For this reason the impious shall not rise in judgment" (those already condemned, since "he who does not believe is already judged"), "nor sinners in the counsel of the just" (those already condemned not to be united with those who have lived unstumbling), "for the Lord knows the way of the just, and the way of the impious shall perish." Again the Lord shows plainly that both the trespasses and the offences are in our power, laying down modes of cure corresponding to the passions, wishing us to be set right by the shepherds, through Ezekiel, blaming certain of them, I think, for the things in which they did not keep the commandments: "The weak you did not strengthen," and the rest, down to "and there was none who sought after nor who turned back"; "for there is great joy with the Father over one sinner saved," says the Lord. By this Abraham is the more praiseworthy, that "he went as the Lord spoke to him."

15.70. From this one of the sages among the Greeks drew the "Follow God." "And the godly," says Isaiah, "took intelligent counsel." And counsel is an inquiry about how we might carry ourselves rightly in present matters, and good counsel is prudence toward deliberations. And what? Does not God too, after the pardon over Cain, in consequence, not much later bring in Enoch the penitent, showing that repentance naturally begets pardon? And pardon is constituted not according to forgiveness, but according to cure. And the same thing happens also in the calf-making of the people under Aaron. From this one of the sages among the Greeks uttered, "Pardon is better than punishment" — just as, indeed, the "Give a pledge, and ruin is at hand" is from the voice of Solomon, which says: "My son, if you give surety for your friend, you will hand over your hand to an enemy; for a man's own lips are a strong snare to him, and he is caught by the words of his own mouth." And more mystically still, the "Know yourself" is taken from there: "You have seen your brother, you have seen your God."

15.71. In this sense, somehow, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself"; "on these commandments," he says, "the whole law and the prophets hang and depend." In harmony with these are those words too: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be fulfilled. And this is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you." "For the Lord is merciful and compassionate, and good is the Lord to all." And more clearly, commending the "Know yourself," Moses says often: "Take heed to yourself." By alms, then, and by faith are sins cleansed away; and "by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil." And "the fear of the Lord is education and wisdom."

16.72. Here again the accusers fasten on, calling joy and grief passions of the soul. For they render joy a reasonable elation, and to exult, to rejoice over noble things; and pity, grief over one suffering ill undeservedly; and they say that such things are changes and passions of the soul. But we, as it seems, do not cease understanding the Scriptures in a fleshly way, and, raising ourselves from our own passions, awaiting the will of the impassible God in likeness to our own motions; supposing that, as we are able to hear, so it is with the Almighty, we wander godlessly. For it was not possible to speak of the divine as it is; but as it was possible for us, fettered in the flesh, to hear, so the prophets spoke to us, the Lord bearing himself with us in a saving way toward the weakness of men.

16.73. Since, then, it is the will of God that the man obedient to the commandments be saved, and the man who repents of his sins, and we rejoice over our salvation, the Lord, who spoke through the prophets, made our gladness his own, just as in the Gospel he says, lovingly toward mankind: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I thirsted, and you gave me to drink; for what you did to one of these least, you did to me." As, then, he is fed without being fed, because the one whom he wishes has been fed, so he rejoiced without being changed, because the one who repented has come to be in joy, as he wished.
