And since God, being good, has mercy richly — giving the commandments through the law, . . . through the prophets, and now more closely through the coming of the Son, saving and having mercy, as has been said, on those who have obtained mercy — and properly the greater has mercy on the lesser; and man would not be greater than man, in so far as he is man by nature, but God is greater than man in all things; if, then, the greater has mercy on the lesser, God alone will have mercy on us. For man becomes social through righteousness and shares what he received from God, both through natural goodwill and relation, and through the commandments which he obeys;

16.74. but God has no natural relation toward us, as the founders of the heresies wish (neither if he should make us from things that are not, nor if he should fashion us from matter — since the one is not at all, and the other is in all respects other than God) — unless one should dare to call us a part of him and of the same essence as God. And I do not know how anyone who has known God will endure to hear this, when he looks at our life, in how many evils we are entangled. For in this way God would be — what it is not even lawful to say — sinning in part, if indeed the parts of the whole are parts and complementary of the whole; and if they are not complementary, neither would they be parts. But, being by nature rich in mercy, through his own goodness God cares for us, though we are neither portions of him nor by nature his children.

16.75. And indeed this is the greatest proof of the goodness of God, that, we being so disposed toward him and by nature wholly estranged, he yet cares for us. For the tender affection toward children is natural to the animals, and the friendship from custom toward those of like mind; but the mercy of God toward us is rich, who belong to him in nothing — I mean by our essence or nature, or by the power proper to our essence — but only by our being the work of his will. And indeed the man who, willingly, with exercise and teaching, has taken up the knowledge of the truth, he calls into adoption, the greatest advance of all. "But lawless deeds hunt down a man, and each is bound fast by the cords of his own sins"; and God is without responsibility. And in truth "blessed is the man who is afraid of all things through caution."

17.76. As, then, knowledge is a state that makes one know, from which the knowing comes about, and the apprehension by it is unwavering by reason, so too ignorance is a yielding impression, changeable by reason; and the changeable, like the thing trained by reason, is in our power. And beside knowledge lie experience and acquaintance, understanding and conception and knowledge. And acquaintance would be a knowledge of universals according to kind; experience a comprehensive knowledge, so as to busy oneself with what each thing is; conception a knowledge of the intelligible; and understanding a knowledge of the comparable, or an unwavering comparison, or a comparative power of the things of which prudence and knowledge are — both of one and of each and of all the things that come into one account; and knowledge a science of the being itself, or a science in harmony with the things that come to be; and truth a knowledge of the true, and the state of the truth a knowledge of true things.

17.77. And knowledge is constituted through reason and is unwavering by another reason. The things we do not do, we either do not do through not being able, or through not wishing, or through both. We do not fly, then, since we neither can nor wish; and we do not, say, swim just now, since we can but do not wish; and we are not as the Lord, since we wish but cannot. For "no disciple is above the teacher; and it is enough if we become as the teacher" — not in essence, for it is impossible for what is so by position to be equal in existence to what is so by nature, but in having become eternal, and in having known the contemplation of the things that are, and in being called sons, and in beholding the Father from the things proper to himself alone. To will, then, leads before all things; for the rational powers are by nature ministers of willing. "Will," it says, "and you will be able." And of the gnostic, the will and the judgment and the exercise are the same. For if the purposes are the same, the doctrines too and the judgments are the same, so that his words and his life and his manner are in keeping with his stand. "And an upright heart seeks out knowledge" and attends to those things. "God has taught me wisdom, and I have known the knowledge of holy things."

18.78. Plain, then, are all the other virtues too, recorded in Moses, that furnished to the Greeks the beginning of the whole ethical sphere — I mean courage and temperance and prudence and justice, and steadfastness and endurance, and gravity and self-control, and the reverence that is upon these. But reverence is plain to everyone, teaching to reverence and honour the highest and most ancient cause. And the law itself presents justice, educating prudence both through the abstinence from the idols of sense and through the allotment to the Maker and Father of the universe, from which opinion, as from a spring, all understanding grows.

18.79. "For the sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of those who walk straight are acceptable with him." Since such too are the things in Isaiah: "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?" says the Lord, and the whole passage. "Loose every bond of injustice"; "for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a contrite heart that seeks its Maker." "Deceitful balances are an abomination before God, but a just weight is acceptable to him." From this Pythagoras advises not to step over the balance. And the profession of the heresies is called a deceitful justice; and "the tongue of the unjust will be utterly destroyed, but the mouth of the just distils wisdom." Yet they call the wise and prudent base. But it would be a long matter to set out testimonies concerning these virtues, since all the Scripture hymns them. Since, then, they define courage as the knowledge of things terrible and not terrible and the things between, and temperance as a state preserving, in choice and avoidance, the judgments of prudence, there lie beside courage both endurance, which they call steadfastness, a knowledge of things to be abided in and not to be abided in, and magnanimity, a knowledge that rises above the things that befall; and beside temperance lies caution, being an avoidance with reason.

18.80. And the keeping of the commandments, being a harmless observance of them, is the gaining of safety in life. And it is not possible to be steadfast without courage, nor self-controlled without temperance. And the virtues follow one another reciprocally; and in whom are the sequences of the virtues, in him is also salvation, being the keeping of the good condition. With reason, then, having further treated of these virtues, we would have considered all of them, since he who has one virtue gnostically has all through the reciprocal following. So self-control is a disposition not to be overstepped of the things that appear according to right reason. And he is self-controlled who holds back the impulses that are against right reason, or who holds himself so as not to be impelled against right reason. And this temperance is not without courage, since it comes about from the commandments, following upon what is ordained . . . by God — prudence and the justice that imitates the divine disposition, according to which, being self-controlled, we are arrayed, pure, toward reverence and the action that consequently follows God, being made like to the Lord so far as is possible for us who are by nature perishable.

18.81. And this is to become just and holy with prudence. For the divine is without need and impassible; whence it is not, properly speaking, self-controlled, for it never falls under passion, that it should master it. But our nature, being passionate, needs self-control, through which, being trained toward the condition of small need, it tries to draw near in disposition to the divine nature. For the earnest man is of small need, on the borderland of immortal and mortal nature, having neediness both through the body and through generation itself, but having been taught to need few things through rational self-control. For what reason has it that the law forbids a man to put on the covering of a woman? Or does it not wish us to be manly, made effeminate neither in body and works nor in thought and reason? For it wishes the man who is at leisure for truth to be made masculine in endurances and steadfastnesses, in life and manner and reason and exercise, by night and by day, and, if there should overtake him the need of a martyrdom that goes through blood.

18.82. Again, if anyone, it says, having lately built a house, has not had time to dwell in it, or, having worked a newly-planted vineyard, has not yet partaken of the fruit, or, having betrothed a virgin, has not yet married her, the law that loves mankind orders these to be released from the campaign — in a generalship-like way, that we may not, distracted toward our desires, serve the war unwillingly (for those are free in their impulses who, without pretext, strip for the dangers); and in a way that loves mankind, since the things of wars are uncertain, having reckoned it unjust that the one should not enjoy his own labours, while another should take, without toil, the things of those who have laboured.

18.83. And the law seems also to show forth the courage of the soul, legislating that the planter should enjoy the fruit, and the builder should dwell, and the betrothed should marry; for it will not make the hopes incomplete to those who have exercised themselves according to the gnostic reason. For of a good man, dead or living, the hope does not perish. "I," it says, "love those who love me," wisdom says; "and those who seek me will find peace," and the rest. And what? Did not the women of the Midianites, warring against the Hebrews by their own beauty, bring them out of temperance, through incontinence, into godlessness? For, having made them their companions out of the grave exercise into harlot-pleasures, and lured them by beauty, they drove them mad toward the sacrifices of the idols and toward foreign women; and, overcome at once by women and by pleasure, they departed both from God and from the law; and well-nigh the whole people had become subject to the enemy by a woman's stratagem, until fear, admonishing, reined them in as they were in danger.

18.84. So those who were left, taking up, in love of danger, the contest for reverence, became masters of the enemy. "The beginning of wisdom, then, is the reverence of God, and the understanding of holy things is forethought, and to know the law belongs to a good understanding." Those, then, who supposed the law to be productive of a passionate fear neither understood as good men nor truly conceived the law. "For the fear of the Lord makes life. But the wanderer will be pained in toils which knowledge does not inspect." Indeed, mystically, Barnabas: "But God, who is Lord of the whole world," he says, "may he give to you too wisdom and understanding, science, knowledge of his ordinances, endurance. Become, then, taught of God, seeking out what the Lord seeks from you, that you may find it in the day of judgment." Those who attain these things he called gnostically children of love and of peace. And concerning sharing and fellowship, there being many discourses, it is enough to say only this: that the law forbids lending to a brother (calling "brother" not only one sprung from the same parents, but anyone who is of the same nation and of like mind and has shared the same reason), thinking it not just to exact interest on money, but to give to those in need with open hands and judgments. For God is the Creator of such a grace; and indeed the man who shares receives notable interest too — the most precious things among men: gentleness, kindness, magnanimity, good report, good fame.

18.85. Does not this precept seem to you to be of love for mankind, as does that one too — to pay the wage of the poor man the same day? It teaches that the wage for services must be paid without delay; for the eagerness of the poor man, who has gone without food, is paralyzed, I think, toward the morrow. Again, it says, let not the creditor stand at the door of the debtor's house, to take a pledge by force, but let the one bid the pledge be brought outside, and let the one who has it not refuse. And in the harvest it forbids the owners to gather up the sheaves that fall, just as in the reaping it advises that something be left uncut, by this very well training the owners toward fellowship and magnanimity, through letting go some of their own to those in need, and furnishing to the poor an occasion of nourishment.

18.86. You see how the legislation announces at once the justice and the goodness of God, who supplies the nourishment to all ungrudgingly? And again, in the vintage, it has forbidden going over again to gather the things left, and to collect the grapes that fall; and the same things it ordains for those who gather olives. Indeed, the tithes too of both the fruits and the flocks taught reverence toward the divine, and not to be wholly lovers of gain, but to share love of mankind with the neighbours too. For from these first-fruits, I think, the priests too were nourished. Do we now understand that we are educated by the law toward reverence and toward fellowship and toward justice and toward love of mankind? Is it not so? Does it not, through the seventh year, command the land to be left idle, and bid the poor freely use the fruits that grow up according to God, nature farming for those who wish? How, then, is the law not good and a teacher of justice? And again, in the fiftieth year, it commands the same things to be accomplished as in the seventh, restoring to each his own, if anyone in the meantime, through some circumstance, was deprived of a plot — limiting the desire of those who long to acquire by a measured time of enjoyment, and having mercy on those who paid the penalty of long poverty and were punished through life. "Alms and faiths are kingly safeguards, and a blessing is upon the head of him who shares"; and "he who has mercy on the poor will be blessed," because he shows love toward his like, through the love toward the Creator of the race of men.

18.87. The aforesaid things have also other, more natural interpretations, concerning rest and the receiving back of the inheritance, but they are not to be told at present. And love is conceived in many ways: through gentleness, through kindness, through endurance, through ungrudgingness and freedom from jealousy, through freedom from hatred, through freedom from remembering wrongs. It is undivided in all things, undiscriminating, social. Again, if you see, it says, the beast of burden of your kindred or friends, or in general of men whom you know, wandering in the desert, lead it away and restore it. And if the master happens to be far off, keep it safe with your own until he recovers it, and restore it. Through natural fellowship it teaches to reckon the find as a deposit, and not to remember wrongs against the enemy.

18.88. "The command of the Lord is a spring of life," truly, "making one turn away from the snare of death." And what? Does it not command us to love the sojourners, not only as friends and kindred, but as ourselves, both in body and in soul? Indeed, it has honoured the nations too, and does not remember evil against those who have done evil. Plainly, then, it says: "You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a sojourner in Egypt" — calling "Egyptian" either the gentile or the whole worldly man. And the enemies, even if they are already standing at the walls trying to take the city, are not yet to be reckoned enemies, until, sending heralds, they summon them to peace. Indeed, with the captive woman too it commands one to consort not for outrage, but, having allowed her to mourn whom she wishes for thirty days, and afterward changing her clothes, "come together with her by law as with a wife"; for it deems that intercourse should come about neither for outrage nor for hire, as with a harlot, but only for the begetting of children.

18.89. You see love of mankind with self-control? To the man who has fallen in love, become master of the captive, it does not permit gratifying his pleasure, but checks the desire by a measured interval, and besides shaves off the captive's hair too, that it may put to shame the outrageous love; for if reasoning persuades to marry, he will hold to her even when she has become unsightly. Then, if anyone, having become sated with the desire, no longer deems it worthy to consort with the captive, it ordains that it is not permitted to sell her, nor even to have her any longer as a handmaid, but wishes her to be free and to be released from servitude, lest, another woman coming in, she suffer something incurable from jealousy.

18.90. And what? Does it command us to help lift and raise up the burden-bearing beasts of enemies too, the Lord teaching us from afar not to welcome rejoicing over evil, nor to take pleasure in the misfortunes of enemies, that, having exercised ourselves in these things, he may teach us to pray for the enemies? For it befits us neither to envy nor to grieve over the goods of the neighbour, nor yet to reap pleasure over the evils of the neighbour. "And if you find a wandering beast of some enemy," it says, "leaving aside the fuel of the quarrel, lead it away and restore it." For upon the forgetting follows nobility, and upon this the dissolution of the enmity. From this we are fitted toward concord, which leads by the hand to happiness. And if you suppose someone an enemy from habit, and overtake him reasoning unreasonably, whether through desire or also through anger, turn him toward nobility.

18.91. Does it now appear that the law is loving of mankind and good, the schoolmaster toward Christ, and that the God who is the same is good with justice, having dealt fittingly, from beginning to end, with each race unto salvation? "Have mercy," says the Lord, "that you may obtain mercy; forgive, that it may be forgiven you; as you do, so it will be done to you; as you give, so it will be given to you; as you judge, so you will be judged; as you show kindness, so kindness will be shown to you; with what measure you measure, it will be measured back to you." Further, it forbids those who serve for food to be dishonoured, and to those enslaved by debts it gives, in the seventh year, a release from everything. But it also forbids handing over suppliants to punishment. So more than anything that oracle is true: "As gold and silver are tried in the furnace, so the Lord chooses the hearts of men." And "the merciful man is long-suffering, and in everyone who takes thought there is wisdom; for thought will fall upon the man of understanding, and, being thoughtful, he will seek life"; and "he who seeks God will find knowledge with righteousness, and those who have rightly sought him found peace."

18.92. And it seems to me that Pythagoras too took the gentleness toward the irrational animals from the law. So he forbade abstaining from the immediate enjoyment of the young born among the flocks and the herds of goats and oxen — not even taking them on the pretext of sacrifices — both for the sake of the offspring and of the mothers, rearing man toward gentleness from below, from the irrational animals. "Grant, then," it says, "to the mother her offspring, even the first seven days." For if nothing comes about without cause, and milk is showered upon those who have given birth for the nourishment of the offspring, the man who drags the newborn away from the dispensation of the milk dishonours nature. Let the Greeks, then, be put to shame, and anyone else who runs down the law, if the one shows kindness even toward irrational animals, while they expose even the offspring of men, though the law, from afar and prophetically, reins in their savagery through the aforesaid commandment. For if it forbids the offspring of the irrational to be separated from the mother before the giving of milk, much more, in the case of men, does it heal beforehand the cruel and untamed mind, that, even if not nature, they may at least not despise learning.

18.93. For to take one's fill of kids and lambs is permitted, and there is perhaps some excuse for the man who separated the offspring from the mother; but what cause has the exposing of a child? For he ought not to have married at all who neither longs to beget children, nor, through incontinence of pleasure, to have become a child-killer. Again, the good law forbids sacrificing offspring and mother on the same day. Hence the Romans too, even if some pregnant woman is condemned to death, do not allow her to undergo the punishment before she has given birth. Plainly, then, of those animals too that are pregnant the law does not permit the slaughtering until they have given birth, restraining from afar the readiness of those who do wrong toward man. Thus it extended the fairness even to the irrational animals, that, having exercised ourselves among the kinds unlike us, we may use, with much abundance of love of mankind, toward the kinds like us.

18.94. But those who, kicking the bellies of certain animals before the birth, that they may feast on flesh mixed with milk, have made the womb, created for generation, a grave of the things carried in it, though the legislator plainly commands: "But you shall not boil a lamb in the milk of its mother"; for, it says, let not the nourishment of the living thing become a seasoning of the slain animal, nor let the cause of life become a co-worker in the consuming of the body. And the same law ordains not to muzzle the ox that threshes; for the worker too must be deemed worthy of food. And it forbids yoking together for the ploughing of the earth an ox and an ass, perhaps aiming at what is unsuited in the animals, but showing at the same time that one must wrong none of the other nations and bring them under the yoke, having nothing to charge except the difference of race, which is without responsibility, springing neither from vice nor from vice. And it seems to me that the allegory also indicates that one must not share the husbandry of the Word equally with the clean and the unclean, the faithful and the unfaithful, because the one is clean, the ox, but the ass has been reckoned among the unclean.

18.95. And, lavishing love of mankind, the good Word teaches that it is not fitting to cut down even those trees that are of cultivated stock, nor to reap the ear unto ruin before the harvest, nor at all to destroy cultivated fruit, neither that of the earth nor that of the soul; for it does not even allow cutting down the country of the enemy. Indeed, husbandmen too have been benefited by the law in these things; for it commands that the newly-planted trees be tended for three years in succession, cutting off the superfluous growths, that they be not weighed down and pressed, and that the nourishment, being not broken up into pieces, not become weak through want, and to mound them up and dig round them, that nothing growing beside hinder the increase. And it does not allow the fruit to be gathered incomplete from the incomplete, but, after three years, in the fourth, to consecrate the first-fruits to God, after the tree has been perfected.

18.96. And this type of husbandry would be a manner of teaching, teaching that one must cut off the side-growths of the sins, and the vain weeds of thought that spring up beside the fruitful fruit, until the shoot of faith be perfected and become firm. For in the fourth year — since there is need of time too for the one securely catechized — the tetrad of the virtues is consecrated to God, the third dwelling now joining on toward the fourth foundation of the Lord. "And a sacrifice of praise is above whole burnt-offerings. For he," it says, "gives you strength to do power. And if matters be enlightened for you, having received and acquired strength in knowledge, do power." For it shows by these things that the good things and the gifts are supplied from God, and that we must, having become ministers of the divine grace, sow the well-doings of God and equip those near us to be noble and good, that as much as possible the temperate man may render the self-controlled, and the courageous the noble, and the prudent and just the understanding and just.

19.97. This is the man according to the image and likeness, the gnostic, who imitates God so far as is possible, leaving out nothing of what tends to the attainable likeness — being self-controlled, enduring, living justly, reigning over the passions, sharing what he has, doing good both in word and in deed so far as he can. "This man," it says, "is greatest in the kingdom, who shall do and teach," imitating God by giving graces like his own; for the gifts of God are for the common benefit. "But whoever undertakes to do anything with arrogance, provokes God," it says; for boastfulness is a vice of the soul, from which, and from the other vices, it commands men to repent, fitting their life out of disharmony toward the better change, through these three: mouth, heart, hands.

19.98. And these would be a symbol: the hands of action, the heart of counsel, and the mouth of speech. Well, then, was that oracle spoken concerning the penitent: "You have chosen God today to be your God, and the Lord has chosen you today to become a people to him." For God makes his own the man who hastens to serve the Being, being a suppliant. And even if he be one in number, he is honoured on a par with the people; for, being a part of the people, he becomes a completion of it, restored from that whence he was; and the whole is also named from a part. And this nobility is shown in the choosing and the joint-exercise of the noblest things. For what did his so great nobility profit Adam? And his father is no mortal; for he himself is the father of men in generation. The shameful things he eagerly chose, following the woman, but the true and noble he neglected; for which he changed a mortal for an immortal life — yet not unto the end.

19.99. But Noah, who did not become as Adam, is saved by divine oversight; for, bringing himself, he offered himself up to God. And Abraham, who begot children by three women, not for the enjoyment of pleasure, but, I think, for the hope of multiplying the race in the beginning — one alone succeeds as heir of the ancestral goods, while the others were settled apart from the kindred. And of twins born from him, the younger inherits, having become well-pleasing to the father, and receives the prayers, while the elder serves him; for the greatest good for the base man is not to be his own master. And this dispensation is both prophetic and typical. And that all things belong to the wise man, he plainly indicates, saying: "Because God has had mercy on me, I have all things." For he teaches that one must reach after one thing, through which all things have come to be, and who apportions the promised things to the worthy.

19.100. He records, then, the earnest man, who has become heir of the kingdom, as a fellow-citizen, through the divine wisdom, of the just men of old too, who lived lawfully both under the law and before the law, whose actions have become laws for us. And again, teaching that the wise man is king, he makes those not of the same nation say to him: "You are a king from God among us" — the ruled, by willing judgment, obeying the earnest man through zeal for virtue. And Plato the philosopher, setting happiness as the end, says it is likeness to God so far as possible — whether running together somehow with the doctrine of the law (for great natures, bare of passions, somehow hit upon the truth, as the Pythagorean Philo says, expounding the things of Moses), or being instructed by certain learned men of that time, as one ever thirsting for learning. For the law says: "After the Lord your God shall you walk, and my commandments shall you keep." For the law names the being-made-like "following"; and such following makes like according to power. "Become," says the Lord, "merciful and compassionate, as your heavenly Father is compassionate."

19.101. From this the Stoics too dogmatized that the end is to live in accordance with nature, having unbecomingly renamed God into nature, since nature extends even to plants and to crops and to trees and to stones. Plainly, then, it is said: "Bad men do not understand law, but those who love law set up for themselves a wall. For the wisdom of the cunning will recognize its ways, but the folly of the foolish is in wandering." "For upon whom shall I look but upon the meek and quiet and him who trembles at my words?" the prophecy says. And we are taught three kinds of friendship; and of these the first and best is that according to virtue, for firm is the love from reason; the second and middle is that according to return — and this is social and giving and useful for life, for common is the friendship from grace; and the last and third we call that from custom, but others that according to pleasure, changeable and variable.

19.102. And it seems to me that Hippodamus the Pythagorean writes most nobly: "Of friendships, the one is from the knowledge of the gods, the one from the giving of men, the one from the pleasure of animals." So the one is the friendship of a philosopher, the one of a man, the one of an animal. For in truth man, doing good, is an image of God, in which he is himself also benefited; for as the pilot at once saves and is saved, so for this reason, when one happens to be asking, one does not say to the giver, "You have given well," but "You have received well." So the giver receives, and the receiver gives. "And the just pity and have mercy; and the kind will be inhabitants of the earth, and the harmless will be left upon it; but the lawless will be utterly destroyed from it." And it seems to me that Homer, foretelling the faithful man, said: "Give to a friend." One must share with a friend, that he may remain still more a friend; and one must aid an enemy, that he may not remain an enemy; for by aid goodwill is bound and enmity dissolved. But if eagerness is set forth, "it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one has not." "For it is not that to others there be relief and to you affliction, but out of equality in the present time," and the rest. "He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness abides forever," says the Scripture. For by the "according to the image and likeness," as we said before too, what is according to the body is not meant — for it is not lawful for a mortal to be made like to the immortal — but what is according to mind and reasoning, upon which the Lord fittingly seals the likeness both toward doing good and toward ruling; for rulings are set right not by the qualities of bodies, but by the judgments of the mind. For "by the counsels of holy men cities are well governed, and a house well ordered."

20.103. And steadfastness too itself forces its way toward the divine likeness, reaping, through endurance, impassivity — if anyone has ringing in his ears the things recorded about those around Ananias, of whom one was Daniel the prophet, filled with divine faith. Daniel dwelt in Babylon, just as Lot in Sodom, and Abraham, who a little after became the friend of God, in the land of the Chaldeans. The king of the Babylonians, then, brought down Daniel into a pit full of beasts, but the king of all, the faithful Lord, brought him up unharmed. This endurance the gnostic, as gnostic, will gain; he will bless when tested, like the noble Job; he will pray, like Jonah, when swallowed by the whale;

20.104. and faith will restore him, prophesying to the Ninevites; and if he be shut up with lions, he will tame the beasts; and if he be cast into fire, he will be bedewed and not be burned up. He will witness by night, he will witness by day; in word, in life, in manner he will witness; being a housemate of the Lord, a familiar and a table-companion according to the spirit, he will remain pure in the flesh, pure in the heart, sanctified in the word. "To this man," it says, "the world is crucified, and he himself to the world." This man, bearing about the cross of the Saviour, follows the Lord "in the track, as of a god," having become a holy one of the holy.

20.105. The divine law, then, making mention of every virtue, anoints man especially toward self-control, laying this down as the foundation of the virtues; and indeed it educates us beforehand toward the gaining of self-control by the use of the animals, forbidding us to partake of all that are by nature fat, like the race of swine, which happens to be very full-fleshed; for such use is supplied to those given to luxury. It is said, at any rate, that one of the philosophers, etymologizing, said the sow (hys) is "for sacrifice" (thyein), as fit only for slaughter and killing; for soul has been given to this animal for nothing else than that its flesh might be plump. Likewise it forbade partaking of the fishes, restraining our desires of those that have neither fins nor scales; for these differ from the other fishes in plumpness and fatness.

20.106. From this, I think, the one who found the rites too forbids touching not only certain animals, but there are also parts even of the sacrificed victims which he excludes from use, for reasons which the initiates know. If, then, one must master the belly and the parts below the belly, it is plain that from above we have received from the Lord, through the law, to cut out desire. And this would come about perfectly, if we should, without dissembling, condemn the fuel of desire — pleasure, I mean. And they say that the notion of it is a smooth and gentle motion with a certain perception. Enslaved to this, they say, Menelaus, after the capture of Ilium, having set out to kill Helen as having become the cause of so many evils, yet was not able to do it, overcome by her beauty, through which he came to the recollection of pleasure.

20.107. Whence, mocking, the tragic poets cried out reproachfully at him: "But you, when you saw the breast, casting away the sword, received a kiss, fawning on the traitorous bitch." And again: "Are swords, then, made dull by beauty?" But I welcome Antisthenes, who says: "Aphrodite I would even shoot down, if I caught her, because she has corrupted many noble and good women of ours." And he calls love a vice of nature; "and the wretched, being weaker than it, call the disease a god." For it is shown by these things that the more unlearned are overcome, through ignorance, by pleasure, which one must not welcome, even if it be called a god — that is, even if it happens to have been given from God toward the need of begetting children. And Xenophon too, plainly calling pleasure a vice, says: "O wretched one, what good do you know, or what noble thing do you regard? You who do not even await the desire of pleasant things, eating before you are hungry, drinking before you are thirsty; and, that you may eat pleasantly, contriving cooks; and, that you may drink pleasantly, preparing costly wines, and in summer running about seeking snow; and, that you may sleep pleasantly, preparing not only soft couches but also stools for the couches."

20.108. Whence, as Ariston said, against the whole tetrachord — pleasure, grief, fear, desire — there is need of much exercise and battle: "For these, these go within the entrails and disturb the heart of men." For even of those who are thought grave, pleasure makes the spirits "waxen," according to Plato, because "each pleasure and grief nails the soul to the body" of the man who does not separate and cross himself off from the passions. "He who has lost his own soul," says the Lord, "will save it" — either giving it over recklessly for the Saviour, as he himself has done for us, or releasing it from fellowship with the accustomed life. For if you should wish to release and remove and separate (for this is what the cross signifies) the soul from the delight and pleasure that is in this life, you will have it found and at rest in the expected hope.

20.109. And this would be the practice of death, if, with the appetites measured according to nature alone, defining nothing beyond the things according to nature toward the more or contrary to nature — where the sinful springs up — we should wish to be content. One must, then, put on the whole armour of God, that we may be able to stand against the methods of the devil, "since the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful with God for the pulling down of strongholds, casting down reasonings and every high thing that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God, and taking captive every thought into the obedience of Christ," says the divine Apostle. There is need of a man who will use, without marvelling and without confusion, the things from which the passions are set in motion — such as wealth and poverty, glory and ill repute, health and disease, life and death, toil and pleasure. For that we may use indifferently the indifferent things, we have need of much discrimination, as having been beforehand harmed by much weakness, and beforehand distorted by bad upbringing and nourishment together with ignorance.

20.110. The simple account, then, of our philosophy says that all the passions are imprints upon the soft and yielding soul, and, as it were, seals impressed by the spiritual powers, against which is our wrestling. For it is the work, I think, of the maleficent powers to try to effect, at each turn, something of their own state, toward overcoming and making their own those who have renounced them. And it follows fittingly that some are thrown down; but those who handle the contest in more athletic fashion, having contended in the all-in struggle and advanced even to the crown, the aforesaid powers, in much gore, then give out, marvelling at the victors. For of the things that move, some are moved by impulse and impression, as the animals, and some by transference, as the lifeless things. And they say that of the lifeless things too the plants are moved by transference toward growth, if one will grant the plants to be lifeless.

20.111. Of state, then, are the stones; of nature, the plants; and of impulse and impression, and again of the two aforesaid, the irrational animals too partake. But the rational power, being proper to the human soul, ought not to be impelled in the same way as the irrational animals, but to discern the impressions and not to be carried away together with them. The powers, then, of which we have spoken, hold out beauties and reputations and adulteries and pleasures and certain such alluring impressions to the easily-led souls, just as those who drive cattle shake green boughs before them; then, having over-reached those unable to discern the true from the false pleasure, and the perishable and outrageous from the holy beauty, they lead them away, having enslaved them. And each deceit, continually pressing upon the soul, imprints in it its image; and so the soul, unawares, bears about the image of the passion, the cause arising both from the bait and from our assent.

20.112. Those about Basilides are wont to call the passions "appendages," and to say that these are certain spirits existing in essence, appended to the rational soul according to a certain original disturbance and confusion; and that other bastard and heterogeneous natures of spirits grow upon these — such as of wolf, ape, lion, goat — whose properties, appearing about the soul, they say make the desires of the soul like to the animals. For of whatever properties they bear, the works of these they imitate; and they not only become akin to the impulses and impressions of the irrational animals, but they emulate even the motions and beauties of plants, because they bear the properties of plants too appended,

20.113. and further the properties of state too, such as the hardness of adamant. But against this doctrine we shall discourse later, when we treat of the soul; now only this must be noted, that the Basilidean man preserves the image of a certain Trojan horse, according to the poetic myth, having enfolded in one body an army of so many different spirits. Indeed, Isidore himself, the son of Basilides, perceiving the doctrine in his work On the Adventitious Soul, as though accusing himself, writes word for word thus: "For if you give anyone a conviction that the soul is not single-part, but that the passions of the worse come about by the violence of the appendages, the base among men will have no ordinary pretext to say: 'I was forced, I was carried off, I acted unwillingly, I worked without wishing it' — they themselves having led the desire of the evils, and not having fought with the violences of the appendages."

20.114. "But one must, having become superior by the reasoning part, appear to master the lesser creation in us." For he too supposes two souls in us, like the Pythagoreans, about whom we shall consider later. But Valentinus too, writing to certain ones, says in these very words concerning the appendages: "There is one good, whose frank manifestation is through the Son, and through him alone the heart can become pure, every wicked spirit being thrust out of the heart. For the many spirits dwelling in it do not allow it to be pure, but each of them accomplishes its own works, outraging it in many ways with desires not fitting. And it seems to me that the heart suffers something like the inn; for that too is bored through and dug up, and often filled with dung by men who lodge in it licentiously and take no forethought for the place, as being another's. In this way the heart too, so long as it has no forethought, is unclean, being a dwelling of many demons; but when the only good Father visits it, it is sanctified and shines with light; and so blessed is the man who has such a heart, for he will see God."

20.115. What, then, is the cause of such a soul's not being provided for from the beginning, let them tell us. For either it is not worthy (and how, then, does the providence approach it, as though from repentance?); or it happens to be a nature saved, as he himself wishes, and then it must from the beginning, being provided for through kinship, give no entrance to the unclean spirits, unless it be forced and convicted of weakness. For if he grants that, having repented, it chooses the better things, this is what he will say unwillingly, the very thing which the truth among us dogmatizes — that salvation comes from an obedient change, and not from nature. For as the exhalations both from the earth and from marshes are constituted into mists and cloudy gatherings, so the risings of the fleshly desires bring an ill state upon the soul, scattering the images of pleasure before the soul.

20.116. They darken, at any rate, the intellectual light, the soul drawing on the risings from desire and thickening the gatherings of the passions by the continuance of pleasures. But a lump of gold is not lifted from the earth, but, being boiled down, is filtered; then, having become pure, it is called gold — earth cleansed. "For ask, and it will be given you," is said to those able of themselves to choose the noblest things. And how we say that the activities of the devil and the unclean spirits sow themselves into the soul of the sinner, I need not many words to present, having set out as witness the apostolic Barnabas (and he was of the seventy and a fellow-worker of Paul), saying somewhat thus, word for word: "Before we believed in God, the dwelling-place of our heart was corruptible and weak, truly a temple built by hand; for it was full of idolatry and was a house of demons, through the doing of all that was contrary to God."

20.117. He says, then, that the sinners accomplish the activities corresponding to the demons, but does not say that the spirits themselves dwell in the soul of the unbeliever. For this reason he adds: "Take heed, that the temple of the Lord be built gloriously. How? Learn. Having received the forgiveness of sins, and having hoped upon the name, let us become new, again created from the beginning." For not the demons are driven out of us, but the sins, he says, are forgiven, which we accomplished, like them, before believing. With reason, then, he set over against this what follows: "Wherefore in our dwelling-place God truly dwells in us. How? His word of faith, his calling of the promise, the wisdom of the ordinances, the commandments of the teaching." I know that I met with a certain heresy, and the one who presided over it asserted, through the use of pleasure, that one must fight pleasure by pleasure — this noble gnostic (for he asserted himself to be a gnostic too) deserting to pleasure through a pretended fight; since, he said, it was no great thing to abstain from pleasure for one who had not tried it, but, being in it, not to be mastered; whence one must exercise through it within it.

20.118. But the wretch, over-reaching himself by the pleasure-loving art, escaped his own notice. To this opinion, evidently, Aristippus of Cyrene too inclined, the sophist who boasted of the truth. Reproached, at any rate, for continually consorting with the Corinthian courtesan, he said: "For I have Lais, and am not had by her." And such too are those who assert themselves to follow Nicolaus, bringing forward a saying of the man, by perversion, that one must abuse the flesh. But the noble man showed that one must cut short both the pleasures and the desires, and by this exercise wither away the impulses and assaults of the flesh. But they, poured out unto pleasure like goats, outraging the body as it were, give themselves to soft living, not knowing that the body wastes away, being by nature in flux, while their soul is buried in the mire of vice — pursuing the doctrine of pleasure itself, and not that of an apostolic man. For in what do these differ from Sardanapallus, whose life the epigram shows: "These I have, all that I ate and outraged and the pleasant things I suffered with love; but those many and blessed things are left behind. For I too am ashes, who reigned over great Ninus." For in general the passion of pleasure is not necessary, but a consequence of certain natural needs — hunger, thirst, cold, marriage.

20.119. If, then, without it one could drink, or take nourishment, or beget children, it would be shown that there is no other need of it. For pleasure is neither an activity nor a disposition, nor any part of us, but came into life for the sake of service, as they say salt does for the sake of the digesting of food. And pleasure, having thrown off the rein and mastered the house, begets the first desire, which is an irrational longing and appetite for what is pleasing to it — which persuaded even Epicurus to set pleasure as the end of the philosopher. He deifies, at any rate, "the stable condition of the flesh and the trustworthy hope concerning it." For what else is luxury but pleasure-loving daintiness and a superfluous excess toward soft living of men given over to it? Plainly Diogenes writes in a certain tragedy: "Those who, in the unmanly and beslimed luxury, stuffed in heart with pleasures, are unwilling to toil even a little." And the things upon these, as many as are shamefully said, yet worthily of the pleasure-lovers.

20.120. Wherefore it seems to me that the divine law necessarily hangs fear over us, that, by caution and attention, the philosopher may gain and keep freedom from anxiety, remaining unstumbling and sinless in all things. For peace and freedom are not otherwise won than through the unceasing and unresting counter-struggle against our passions . . . For these antagonists are stout and Olympic, sharper, so to speak, than wasps — and especially pleasure, which not only by day but also by night, in the very dreams, plots and bites alluringly with sorcery. How, then, are the Greeks any longer just in running down the law, when they themselves too teach the enslaving of pleasure by fear? Socrates, at any rate, commands to guard against the things that persuade us to eat when not hungry and to drink when not thirsty, and the glances and kisses of the beautiful, as fit to inject a venom worse than that of scorpions and spiders.

20.121. And Antisthenes too chooses rather to go mad than to feel pleasure; and Crates the Theban says: "But of these be master by a soul exulting in character, neither enslaved by gold nor by love that melts with longing, nor if there be any companion of outrage." And in sum he adds: "Unenslaved and unfulled by slavish pleasure, they love the immortal kingdom and freedom." The same man writes elsewhere outright that the poultice for the uncontrollable impulse toward the things of love is hunger, and, if not, a noose. And to Zeno the Stoic the comic poets bear witness of his teaching, though deriding it, somewhat thus: "For this man philosophizes a new philosophy: he teaches hunger and gets disciples; one loaf, dried figs for relish, and water to drink upon them."

20.122. All these, then, are not ashamed plainly to confess the benefit that comes from caution. But the true and not irrational wisdom, trusting not in bare oracles and divinations, but in shelters that cannot be wounded and in effective mysteries, the divine commandments, . . . practising itself by joint-exercise and joint-training, receives a divine power according to the part of it that is inspired by the Word. So already they write of the aegis of the poetic Zeus that it is terrible, "about which on all sides Fear is wreathed; in it is Strife, in it Valour, in it chilling Pursuit; and in it the Gorgon head of the dread monster, terrible and grim, the portent of aegis-bearing Zeus."

20.123. To those able rightly to discern the saving thing, I do not know if anything will appear dearer than the gravity of the law and its daughter, caution. But when it is said to sing "too high a pitch" — as the Lord too sang to certain ones, that none of those who emulate him might sing out of pitch and off the string — I understand it thus: not as too high a pitch, but to those unwilling to take up the divine yoke it is too high a pitch. For to the slack and weak the moderate seems too high, and to the unjust the fitting seems extremely just. For all whom pardon enters in because of their friendly disposition toward sins, these suppose the truth to be harshness, and the austerity severity, and the man who neither sins with them nor is dragged down with them, merciless.

20.124. Well, then, does the tragedy write concerning Hades: "And to what a god you will come, as to a Love that knew neither fairness nor grace, but cherished only bare justice." For even if you are not yet able to do the things commanded by the law, yet, perceiving that the noblest examples lie before us in it, we can nourish and increase the love of freedom; and here too we would be benefited, more eagerly, according to our power, in some things calling ourselves on, in some imitating, in some too being put to shame. For neither were the just men of old, who lived according to the law, "from oak of olden tale or from rock"; but by their willing to philosophize genuinely, bearing themselves whole, they offered themselves up to God, and it was reckoned unto faith.

20.125. Most nobly Zeno said of the Indians that he would rather see one Indian roasted than learn all the demonstrations about pain. But to us there are ungrudging springs of witnesses, beheld every day before our eyes, roasted, impaled, having their heads cut off. All these the fear from the law, having schooled them toward Christ, trained to display their caution even through bloods. "God stood in the assembly of gods, and in the midst he will judge gods." Who are these? Those superior to pleasure, those who surpass the passions, those who know each thing they do, the gnostics, those greater than the world. And again, "I said, you are gods, and all sons of the Most High." To whom does the Lord speak? To those who decline, so far as may be, all that is human. And the Apostle says: "For you are no longer in the flesh, but in the spirit." And again he says: "Being in the flesh, we war not according to the flesh; for flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption; but behold, you die as men" — the Spirit has said this, convicting us.

20.126. One must, then, train oneself toward caution about the things that fall under the passions, banishing, as the true philosophers do, the foods that lead to passion, and the slack relaxation at the bed, and luxury and the passions toward luxury, . . . a heavy contest to others, but to us no longer; for self-control is the greatest gift of God. For he himself has said, "I will not loose you, nor will I forsake you," having judged us worthy on account of our genuine choice. So, when we try to approach cautiously, the good yoke of the Lord will receive us, "from faith to faith," one charioteer driving each of us, according to advance, toward salvation, that the fitting fruit of happiness may result. And, according to Hippocrates of Cos, exercise is not only of the body, but also of the soul: "health is freedom from sluggishness in toils, freedom from satiety in food."

21.127. But Epicurus, setting the happiness equal to the gods in the not being hungry nor thirsty nor cold, uttered, speaking impiously, "In these things I would fight even with father Zeus" — dogmatizing a blessed victory of dung-eating pigs, and not of rational and philosophic beings. For of those who begin from pleasure . . . are the Cyrenaics and Epicurus; for these say outright that the end is to live pleasantly, and that pleasure alone is the perfect good. And Epicurus says that the removal of pain too is pleasure; and he says that to be chosen is what first, of itself, draws toward itself, being plainly in motion. And Dinomachus and Calliphon said the end is to do all that depends on oneself for the sake of attaining and obtaining pleasure; and Hieronymus the Peripatetic said the end is to live without disturbance, but the final good is happiness alone. And Diodorus likewise, being of the same school, declares the end to be to live without disturbance and nobly.

21.128. Epicurus, then, and the Cyrenaics say the first thing proper is pleasure; for virtue, they say, came in for the sake of pleasure and produced pleasure. But according to those about Calliphon, virtue entered in for the sake of pleasure, but afterward, in time, having beheld the beauty about it, presented itself as of equal honour with the beginning — that is, with pleasure. But those about Aristotle render the end to be living according to virtue, but say that neither happiness nor the end is present to everyone who has virtue; for the wise man, when tortured and falling into unwished-for fortunes, and on account of these willingly wishing to escape from life, is neither blessed nor happy. For virtue too needs some time; for it does not result in one day, and it is constituted in a perfect being, since, as they say, a child is never happy; and the perfect time would be the human life. Happiness, then, is filled up out of the threefold kind of goods. So neither the poor, nor the obscure, nor the sickly, nor, if anyone be a slave, is happy, according to them. . . .

21.129. Again, Zeno the Stoic holds the end to be living according to virtue; Cleanthes, living in agreement with nature; and Diogenes held the end to lie in good reasoning, which he took to lie in the choosing of the things according to nature. And Antipater, his pupil, supposes the end to lie in continually and inviolably choosing the things according to nature and rejecting the things contrary to nature. And Archedemus again thus expounded the end to be, living, choosing the greatest and most authoritative things according to nature, which it is not possible to overstep. Besides these, Panaetius declared the end to be living according to the occasions given us from nature. And above all, Posidonius declared the end to be living, contemplating the truth and order of the universe, and helping to constitute it so far as possible, being led in nothing by the irrational part of the soul. And some of the younger Stoics rendered it thus: that the end is to live in keeping with the constitution of man. Why should I reckon up Ariston for you? He said the end is indifference; but the indifferent simply leaves the indifferent. Or should I bring into the midst the things of Herillus? He sets the end to be living according to knowledge. For some hold that the younger ones from the Academy render the end to be the secure withholding of judgment toward the impressions. Indeed, Lyco the Peripatetic said the true joy of the soul is the end, as Leucimus said the joy over noble things. And Critolaus, himself too a Peripatetic, said it is the perfection of a life flowing well according to nature, indicating the threefold perfection filled up out of the three kinds.

21.130. We must not, then, stop, contenting ourselves with these things, but must be as ambitious as possible to set out also the things dogmatized by the natural philosophers about the matter before us. For they say that Anaxagoras of Clazomenae said that the end of life is contemplation and the freedom that comes from it; and Heraclitus of Ephesus, well-pleasing. And Heraclides of Pontus relates that Pythagoras handed down that the science of the perfection of the numbers of the soul is happiness. But the Abderites too teach that there is an end: Democritus, in his work On the End, cheerfulness, which he also called "well-being" (and he often adds: "For delight and lack of delight are the boundary of things at their height"); and Hecataeus, self-sufficiency; and Apollodotus of Cyzicus, leading of the soul, as Nausiphanes, freedom from astonishment — for this, he said, was called by Democritus "freedom from amazement." Further, besides these, Diotimus declared the all-completeness of goods, which is named "well-being," to be the end. Again, Antisthenes said freedom from conceit; and those called Annicereans, from the Cyrenaic succession, set down no defined end of the whole life, but said that of each action the proper end is the pleasure that results from the action. These Cyrenaics reject Epicurus' definition of pleasure — that is, the removal of pain — calling it the condition of a corpse; for we rejoice not only over pleasures, but also over companionships and ambitions. But Epicurus thinks that all joy of the soul comes about upon the flesh as primarily affected.

21.131. And Metrodorus, in his work On the fact that the cause in ourselves toward happiness is greater than that from things, says: "What good of the soul is there other than the stable condition of the flesh and the trustworthy hope concerning it?"

22.131. Indeed, Plato the philosopher says the end is twofold: the one participable and primary, existing in the very forms — which he also names "the Good"; and the one participating in that and receiving the likeness from it, which comes about among men who lay claim to virtue and the true philosophy. Wherefore Cleanthes too, in the second book On Pleasure, says that Socrates taught at every turn that the same man is both just and happy, and cursed the first man who divided the just from the advantageous, as having done an impious thing; for in truth impious are those who separate the advantageous from the just that is according to law. And Plato himself says that happiness is "to have the daimon well" (eu ton daimona echein), and that the governing part of our soul is called daimon, and that happiness is the most perfect and fullest good. And sometimes he calls it a life that is in agreement and harmony, and sometimes the most perfect according to virtue; and this he sets in the knowledge of the Good and in the being made like to God — declaring the likeness to be to become just and holy with prudence. For is it not so that some of our own people take it that man received the "according to the image" straightway at his generation, but is to receive the "according to the likeness" later, at his perfecting?

22.132. So Plato, teaching that this likeness will come to the virtuous man with humility, somewhere interprets that saying: "Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted." He says, at any rate, in the Laws: "God, then, as the ancient saying too has it, holding the beginning and the middle and the end of all things, brings them to fulfilment by a straight course, going round according to nature; and upon him there ever follows Justice, the avenger of those who fall short of the divine law." You see how he too brings caution toward the divine law? So he adds: "To which the man who is to be happy clings and follows, humble and adorned." Then, having joined the things that follow upon these, and having admonished by fear, he adds: "What action, then, is dear to and follows God? One, and having one ancient saying: that the like is dear to the like, being measured; but the unmeasured is dear neither to one another nor to the measured. The man, then, who is to become dear to God must of necessity become, so far as possible, such a one himself."

22.133. And according to this account the temperate man among us is dear to God, for he is like; and the man not temperate is unlike and different. Having said that this doctrine is ancient, he hinted at the teaching that came to him from the law. And in the Theaetetus, having granted that the evils about mortal nature and this place go round of necessity, he adds: "Wherefore one must try to flee from here to there as quickly as possible; and the flight is likeness to God so far as possible; and the likeness is to become just and holy with prudence." And Speusippus, the nephew of Plato, says that happiness is a perfect state in those who are according to nature, or a state of goods, of which condition all men have appetite, but the good aim at freedom from disturbance. And the virtues would be productive of happiness. And Xenocrates of Calchedon renders happiness the possession of one's own virtue and of the power that serves it. Then, as that in which it comes to be, he plainly says the soul; as that by which, the virtues; as that out of which, as of parts, the noble actions and the earnest states and dispositions and motions and relations; and as those without which it is not, the bodily and external things. For Polemo, the pupil of Xenocrates, plainly wishes happiness to be self-sufficiency in all goods, or in the most and greatest. He dogmatizes, at any rate, that without virtue happiness can never exist, but that, apart from the bodily and external things, virtue is self-sufficient toward happiness.

22.134. And let these things be so; but the refutations of the opinions stated will be set down in due time. For us ourselves it is set forth to come to an endless end, obeying the commandments — that is, God — and having lived according to them blamelessly and with knowledge, through the knowledge of the divine will. And the likeness, so far as possible, to right reason is the end; and the restoration, through the Son, to the perfect adoption, which ever glorifies the Father through the great High Priest, who deigned to call us brothers and joint-heirs. And the Apostle, briefly describing the end in the Epistle to the Romans, says: "But now, freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end eternal life." And, knowing hope to be twofold — the one expected, the other received back — he teaches that the restoration of hope is already the end; "for endurance," he says, "works proof, and proof hope; and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us." On account of which love is also the restoration to the hope, which he elsewhere says is laid up for us as a rest.

22.135. The like you would find in Ezekiel too, running thus: "The soul that sins, it shall die. And a man who becomes just and does judgment and righteousness, who has not eaten upon the mountains, and has not lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, and has not defiled his neighbour's wife, and has not approached a woman in the separation of her uncleanness" (for he does not wish the sowing of man to be outraged), "and, it says, has not oppressed a man, will restore the debtor's pledge, will not seize plunder, will give his bread to the hungry, and will clothe the naked, will not give his money at interest, and will take no excess, will turn his hand from injustice, will do true judgment between a man and his neighbour, will walk in my ordinances and has kept my ordinances to do truth — he is just, he shall surely live, says the Lord Adonai." And Isaiah, exhorting the believer toward gravity of life, but the gnostic toward attention, presenting that the virtue of man and of God is not the same, says thus: "Seek the Lord, and in finding him call upon him; and when he draws near to you, let the impious leave his ways, and the lawless man his ways, and let him turn to the Lord, and he will obtain mercy,"

22.136. "for your thoughts are far from my thought." We, then, according to the noble Apostle, await from faith the hope of righteousness. "For in Christ neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love." "And we desire each of you to show the same diligence toward the full assurance of hope," down to "having become, according to the order of Melchizedek, a high priest forever." The like to Paul the all-virtuous Wisdom too says: "But he who hears me will dwell upon hope, trusting"; for the restoration of hope is called, by the same name, "hope"; wherefore to the word "will dwell" it most nobly added "trusting," showing that such a one is at rest, having received back the hope which he hoped; wherefore it adds: "and he will be at ease, without fear, from every evil." And plainly the Apostle, in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, says outright: "Become imitators of me, as I also am of Christ" — that that might come about: "if you are mine, and I am Christ's, then become imitators of Christ, and Christ of God." The being made like to God, then, so far as was possible — to become just and holy with prudence — he lays down as the aim of faith, and as the end the restoration of the promise that is upon faith. From these, then, gush the springs of those who dogmatized about the end, which we have spoken of before. But enough of these.

23.137. Since marriage seems to fall under pleasure and desire, we must treat of this too. Marriage, then, is the first union of man and woman according to law, for the sowing of legitimate children. So the comic poet Menander says: "For the begetting of legitimate children I give you my own daughter." And we inquire whether one should marry, which is one of the things named as somehow "in relation to something." For who should marry, and being in what condition, and whom, and being in what condition? For neither should everyone marry, nor at all times; but there is a time in which it is fitting, and a person to whom it befits, and an age up to which. So neither should everyone marry every woman, nor at all times, nor at all, nor without restraint, but the man in a certain condition, and such a woman as he ought, and when he ought, and for the sake of children, and one in all respects like-minded, and not loving the husband by force or necessity.

23.138. Whence Abraham says concerning his wife, pretending her to be his sister: "She is my sister by my father, but not by my mother; and she became my wife also" — teaching that those of the same mother must not be taken in marriage. Let us run over the history in brief. Plato sets marriage among the external goods, providing for the immortality of our race and a kind of continuance, as it were, handed down like a torch through children's children. But Democritus declines marriage and the begetting of children, on account of the many unpleasantnesses from them and the distractions from more necessary things. And Epicurus too is ranged with him, and all who set the good in pleasure and freedom from disturbance, and further in freedom from grief. Further, according to those from the Stoa, marriage and child-rearing are indifferent, but according to those from the Peripatos a good. In sum, these, having brought their doctrines as far as the tongue, were enslaved to pleasures — some using concubines, some courtesans, and most of them boys. And that wise tetrad in the garden, with the courtesan, gloried in pleasure by their works.

23.139. So they would not escape the Buzygian curse, all who, not approving certain things as advantageous to themselves, enjoin upon others to do these, or, again, the contrary. This the Scripture has shown briefly, saying: "What you hate, you shall not do to another." But those who approve marriage say: Nature has made us well-fitted for marriage, as is plain from the constitution of the bodies, both of the males and of the females; and they continually cry out the "Increase and multiply." And even if these things are so, yet let it seem shameful to them that man, fashioned by God, should be more incontinent than the irrational animals, which do not mingle with many and without restraint, but with one and of their own kind — such as the wild pigeons and the ring-doves and the race of turtle-doves and the like. Further, they say, the childless man falls short of the perfection according to nature, as not having set in his own place a successor of his own; for the perfect man is one who has made from himself the like, or rather, when he sees that one too having done the same — that is, when he has set the begotten into the same nature as the begetter.

23.140. One must, then, by all means marry, both for the sake of the fatherland, and for the succession of children, and for the completing of the world, so far as in us lies. Since the poets too pity a certain marriage that is half-finished and childless, but bless the one with both parents flourishing. And the bodily diseases especially show marriage to be necessary; for the care of the wife and the intensity of her staying-by seem to surpass the perseverances of the other kindred and friends, by as much as she chooses to differ in sympathy and to attend most of all; and in truth, according to the Scripture, she is a necessary helper.

23.141. So the comic poet Menander, having run down marriage, but setting against it also the useful things, answers the one who said: "I am ill-disposed toward the matter." "B: For you take it the wrong way." Then he adds: "You see in it the troublesome things and those that will grieve you, but you do not look upon the goods," and the rest. And marriage helps also in the case of those advanced in time, presenting the wife who cares, and rearing the children from her as nurses of old age. "And children, to a man who has died, are tokens of fame; like corks they hold up the net, saving the spun line of flax from the deep," according to the tragic Sophocles. And the lawgivers do not allow those who have not married to seek the greatest offices. So the lawgiver of the Spartans set a penalty not only for celibacy, but for bad marriage and late marriage and solitary living. And the noble Plato commands that the man who has not married pay the maintenance of a wife to the public treasury, and render the fitting expenses to the magistrates. For if men who do not marry will not beget children, they will, so far as in them lies, make a scarcity of men, and dissolve both the cities and the world that is from them.

23.142. And such a thing is impious, of men dissolving the divine generation. And it is, besides, unmanly and weak to flee the common life with wife and children. For of that whose loss is an evil, the possession is altogether a good; and so it is with the rest too. But indeed the loss of children is among the greatest evils, they say. The possession of children, then, is a good. And if this, then marriage too. "And without a father," he says, "there could never be a child, and without a mother not even the conception of a child."

23.143. And marriage makes a father, as a man makes a mother. So Homer too sets it as the greatest prayer, "a husband and a house" — but not simply, but "with noble like-mindedness"; for the marriage of others is of one mind toward soft living, but that of those who philosophize leads to the concord according to reason — the marriage that bids the women adorn not their form but their character, and does not enjoin the men to use their wives as mistresses, having made the outrage of bodies their aim, but to win marriage as a help in the whole of life and the best temperance. For of wheat, I think, and of barley too, cast down at their proper seasons, more precious is the man who is sown, for whom all things grow; and those seeds the husbandmen cast down sober. Everything filthy and defiled in conduct, then, must be purified away from marriage, that we be not reproached with the union of the irrational animals as agreeing more with nature than human wedlock, according to the agreed definition.

23.144. Some of them, at any rate, having mounted at the season commanded, straightway depart, leaving the creation to the administration. And by the tragic poets Polyxena, though she is being slaughtered, is recorded — even dying, yet to have taken much forethought to fall decently, "hiding what must be hidden from the eyes of males." And for her too the calamity was a marriage. To fall under, then, and to yield to the passions is the utmost slavery, just as, indeed, to master these is the only freedom. So the divine Scripture says that those who transgress the commandments are "sold to strangers" — that is, to sins unsuited to nature — until, turning back, they repent.

23.145. Marriage, then, must be kept pure, like some sacred image, from the things that defile it — by those who rise from sleep with the Lord, and go to sleep with thanksgiving and prayer, "both when you lie down and when the holy light comes," calling the Lord to witness throughout the whole of our life — having gained godliness in the soul, and bringing temperance even to the body. For it is in truth dear to God to lead orderliness by the hand from the tongue to the works; and the way to shamelessness is shameful speech, and the end of both is shameful deed. And that the Scripture counsels marrying, and never permits departing from the wedlock, it plainly legislates: "You shall not put away your wife, except for the matter of fornication"; and it reckons it adultery to marry again while either of the separated is living.

23.146. And it shows a woman unsuspected of slander by her not adorning herself, nor decking herself beyond what is fitting, but devoting herself earnestly to prayers and supplications; guarding against the many goings-out of the house, and shutting herself off so far as possible from the sight of those to whom she does not belong, holding housekeeping more important than untimely chatter. "And he who takes a divorced woman commits adultery," it says; "for if anyone puts away his wife, he makes her commit adultery" — that is, he forces her to be adulterated. And not only the man who puts her away becomes the cause of this, but also the man who takes her in, furnishing the woman an occasion of sinning; for if he did not receive her, she would turn back to her husband.

23.147. What, then, does the law do? For the checking of the proneness of the passions, it commands the adulteress, when convicted of this, to be put to death; and if she be a priest's daughter, it commands her to be given over to fire. And the adulterer too is stoned, but not in the same place, that not even their death be common. The law does not, then, fight with the Gospel, but agrees with it. For how should it not, the supplier of both being one, the Lord? For she who has played the harlot lives indeed to sin, but has died to the commandments; while she who has repented, as though reborn through the turning of her life, has a regeneration of life, the old harlot having died, and the woman born according to repentance having come again into life. The Spirit bears witness to what has been said, through Ezekiel, saying: "I do not wish the death of the sinner, so much as his turning back." So they are stoned, as having died, through hardness of heart, to the law which they did not obey; but for the priest's daughter the punishment is intensified, because "to whom more was given, of him will also more be required." Let this second Miscellany too be here circumscribed for us, on account of the length and multitude of the chapters.
